The chapter on the introduction to the tantra.
On the glorious Mahendra mountain, which brings delight to the eyes of the world,
there were *kalpavṛkṣa*, *śamī*, *vaṭa*, *campaka*, and *pippala* trees.
In a great golden assembly hall, perfumed with sandalwood along with *plakṣa* and *punnāga* trees, and adorned with all varieties of precious materials. || 2 ||
In the great forest, upon a lion-throne adorned as a locus of auspiciousness,
sat the Supreme Lord, who transcends the reach of speech and mind.
The God of gods, the great treasure, liberated from beginningless impurity,
the ordainer of all sciences, accompanied by Gaurī on his left.
It was served by Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, the Sun, the Moon, sages, and Gandharvas,
and was being praised by the gods and others with auspicious hymns of praise.
To the gracious Supreme Lord, the Sovereign whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon,
Maheśvara, being himself serene in soul, offered his longing desire to receive the knowledge of Śiva.
Having first bowed with devotion and great respect, Maheśvara spoke these words for the benefit of the world:
"O God of gods, Lord of the universe, destroyer of the afflictions of your devotees! (7)
O Lord of creation, preservation, destruction, and grace;
O Knower of that which extends from the end of Śiva to the end of the ocean; O Revealer of the blood of knowledge! || 8 ||
O Compassionate-faced One, skilled in untying the bonds of the fettered,
[I pray] with supreme devotion whose nature is the realization of the Supreme Consciousness.
O Śambhu, omniscient one, doer of all, soul of all, facing every direction!
[This is] beneficial for practitioners, meritorious, and the means to liberation for yogins. || 10 ||
"O Supreme Lord, tell me the supreme, pure knowledge of Śiva. Thus questioned by Maheśa, the Blessed Supreme Lord [spoke].
(PDF 5, p.
649) In the *Sarvalokahitaiṣiṇī*, the Supreme Lord spoke with a profound voice:
I shall explain according to the path of brevity, in accordance with the question and as desired.
O illustrious Maheśvara, listen with a concentrated mind to the supreme, secret Śiva-knowledge, which is auspicious and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 13.
This meritorious work removes all sins, provides understanding of the essential meaning of the Tantras, and, consisting of one hundred thousand verses, accomplishes all goals. (14)
O Great Lord, that great tantra called the Makuṭa, which belongs to the Upper Śaiva tradition, shall now be proclaimed to you in brief. (15)
Now, listen briefly and in order to the ninefold Śaiva [tradition]: first is the Ūrdhvaśaiva, and the second is the Ādiśaiva. || 16 ||
The third is the Anādiśaiva; the fourth is the Anuśaiva;
the fifth is the Avāntara; and the sixth is indeed the Miśra. || 17 ||
The seventh is the Bheda-Śaiva, the eighth is the Guṇa-Śaiva, and the ninth is the Ājñā-Śaiva; listen now to this sequence of the divisions of Śaivism.
The Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula traditions constitute the fourfold [division].
Among these, the Śaiva is the most excellent, arising from the Upper Current (ūrdhvasrotas).
Then, the Śaiva [tradition] is said to be of two kinds: the gentle (saumya) and the fierce (raudra).
The gentle is declared to be of two types: the right-hand (dakṣiṇa) and the mixed (miśraka).
Conduct known from the Vedas is called Dakṣiṇācāra;
the opposite is Vāmācāra, while the mixture of the two is Saṅgama.
This Tantra is the essence of the Vedas; therefore, one should practice according to the Vedic way.
This knowledge, consisting of the meaning of Vedanta, is the supreme and auspicious Siddhanta.
(From PDF 6, p.

650) The *Aṣṭāviṃśatitantra* is the most excellent, arising from the *Ūrdhvasrotas*; it should be known as that which bestows the essential meaning of the Vedas, while others are means for different purposes. (23)

At the beginning of the Tantra, the *Tantrasadbhāva*, which consists of the root divisions and sub-divisions, shall be described by its names, starting with the *Kāmika*; listen as it is explained in sequence. (24)
It extends vast benefits based on reality and mantra, and it provides protection for persons; therefore, it is known as "tantra. (25)
Kāmika, Yogaja, Cintya, and likewise Ajita as the cause;
Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumān, and Suprabhedaka.
Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svāyaṃbhuva, Amayānala, Vīra, Raurava, and likewise Makuṭa and Vimala.
The Candrajñāna, the Bimba, the Prodgīta, the Lalita, as well as the Siddha known as the Santāna, and the Pārameśvara spoken by Śarva. (28)
The Kirāṇa and the Vātula—these are the twenty-eight Saṃhitās;
among these, the first ten are proclaimed as the divisions of Śiva. (29)
Likewise, there is another eighteen-fold division known by the names of the Rudras;
the Śivarudra-tantra consists of twenty-eight [parts].
Although the speaker arises from a single source, he appears in many ways due to the diversity of listeners;
this is especially true for the listeners of the Siddhānta and Tantra scriptures. (31)
O Maheśvara, listen as I proclaim those beginning with Praṇava;
there are three lineages of listeners for each of the divisions of Śiva.
The sixty-six varieties of Rudras have been declared in pairs:
Praṇava, Trikalā, Tryakṣa, Sudhākhya, Bhasmaka, and Vibhu. (33)
(From PDF 7, p.
651) Sudīpta, Gopati, and afterwards Ambikā as the cause; Śarva, Rudra, Prajeśa, Subhu, Śivaśiva, and Acyuta. || 34 ||
Īśa, named Trimūrti, and Hutāśa known as Sūkṣma;
then indeed Śravaṇa, and Prabha, which is designated as Jñā. || 35 ||
Kāla, Bhīma, Dharma, Tatogra, and the one named Ambu;
Ravi, Vighneśvara, Dadhīśa, and the one named Śiva. (36)
The presiding deities of the thirty divisions of Śiva have been declared in their proper sequence:
Anādi, Parameśa, Daśārṇa, and then Girijā. (37)
Nidhana, Padmasambhūta, Vyomanāman, Agnisaṃjñaka, Tejas, Prajāpati, Prameṇas, and Naghnaka. || 38 ||
Śiva, Mahādeva, Sarvātmā, Vīrabhadraka, Ananta, Bṛhaspati, Praśānta, and Dadhīcaka; || 39 ||
Then Śūlin, Kavaca, Ālaya, Rudrabhairava, Bindu, Caṇḍeśvara, and Śivaniṣṭha along with Savoplava. || 40 ||
Somadeva, Nṛsiṃha, Śrīdevī, Uśanas, Devapītā, Saṃvarta, Śiva, and Mahākāla; || 41 ||
The enumeration of the principles (tattvas), the divisions of Rudra, and the presiding deities,
as well as the root tantras and their sub-divisions, shall be declared in order by name.
The Kāmika is said to have three divisions, the Yogaja five,
the Cintya Tantra six, and the Kāraṇa seven.
That which is called Ajita has four divisions; Dīpta has nine divisions;
Sūkṣma is said to be of one kind; and Sahasraka has ten divisions.
(From *pdf* 8, p. 652):
Aṃśumān is the division of the Sūrya [Tantra]; Suprabheda is the non-differentiated [division].
Vijaya is the eightfold division, and Niśvāsa is likewise the eightfold division. (45)
The Svāyambhuva has two divisions, and the Āgneya likewise has two divisions;
the Vīratantra, in particular, has thirteen divisions. (46)
Raurava is said to have six divisions, while Makuṭa has two;
Vimala has the division of Kalā, and Candrajñāna has fourteen.
The *Tithibheda*, the *Bimbatantra*, and the *Prodgīta*—these sixteen are remembered;
then there would be the *Lalita* which is the *Guṇabheda*, and the *Siddha* which is the *Yugabheda*. (48)
In the Santāna [Tantra], there are seven divisions; that spoken by Śarva consists of five.
The Parameśa has seven divisions, and the Kiraṇa has nine. (49)
The Vātula and the Ravibheda shall be [described], and they will be explained individually; likewise the Nārasiṃha, the Vaktāra, and the Bhairavottara. (50)
The Kāmika has three divisions: Sāra, Vīṇāśikhottara, and Ātmayoga; Sūtāra is the fourth, and Yoga is the fifth.
Sucintya, Subhaga, Vāma, Amṛta, and Pāpanāśana—
these six divisions of Cintya, which arises from Parā, are proclaimed in sequence.
Mahendra, Kāraṇa, Yoga, Pāvana, Himasaṃhita, Vidveṣa, and Māraṇa—these are the seven varieties within the Kāraṇa [type]. (53)
And there is the Prabhūta, the Svarodbhūta, and that which is composed by the Lord of Pārvatī;
then the four divisions of Ajita, followed by the innumerable Abja.
If one perceives that which is being consumed as the immeasurable,
possessed of supreme splendor, the wonderful manifestation of Mādhava, then they have forgotten the radiant Tantra.
In the subtle tantras, that which is called "subtle" is proclaimed as the very *rāka*.
It is transcendent, auspicious, pure, immeasurable, and possesses the nature of the *jāti*. (56)
The awakened, the wise, the hand-ornament, and the well-enlightener;
ten divisions of the *Sahasra-tantra* have been proclaimed. (57)
The Kāśyapa, the Vāsava, the Aindra, the Vāsiṣṭha, and likewise the Gautama;
the Bhūtatantra-prakaraṇa and the Vidya-purāṇa as well. || 58 ||
And the one known as Īśānottara, as well as Nīlalohita;
the Self, the Adornment, and Brahman are beneficial for the ten-rayed one. (59)
The *Suprabheda*, however, is non-differentiation; it is the origin of the wealth of Kubera, most terrible yet non-terrible, stainless, and the destroyer of death. (60)
And the eight divisions of that which is known as Vijaya are proclaimed:
Niśvāsa, Mantraniśvāsa, and the one named Niśvāsottara; || 61 ||
The horse has its origin in the breath; it is the maker of the horse's breath.
It is indeed the path of the breath and arises from the mouth of the breath. 62.
The eight divisions of the Niśvāsa are proclaimed as belonging to the Mahātantra;
both the Prājāpatya and the Padma are remembered as being within the Svāyambhuva.
The Āgneya [system] is declared to be twofold: the Āgneya and the Vyomatantraka.
[Its components are] Bodha, Prabodha, Śakaṭa, Bodhaka, Prastara, and Hala. (64)
The Bhadra, Vilekhana, Vīra, Mohana, Śākaṭāyika, as well as the Phullanayana and the Mohasaṃbhava. || 65 ||
O Maheśvara, thirteen divisions have been proclaimed in the Vīratantra:
Kāladāha, Kalātīta, Raurava, and Rauravottara; || 66 ||
The Mahākālamata, the Cāndra, and the six divisions of the Raurava;
two divisions are proclaimed in the Makuṭa: the Mākuṭa and the Mākuṭottara. (67)
Vṛṣabha, Vṛṣapiṅgākṣa, Mātrānta, Vṛṣabhottara, Sudanta, Atibhūta, Raudra, and likewise Bhadravita. (68)
Ārevana, known as Subhadra, Atikrānta, Alaṅkṛta, Ananta, Aṭṭahāsa, Accita, and likewise Māraṇa. || 69 ||
Thus, sixteen divisions of the Vimalatantra have been proclaimed:
the Rākapādapurāṇa, the one called Sthāṇu, and the Nandikeśvara. (70)
The one called Sthira, proclaimed by Śaṅkara, Śrīmukha, Śivabhadra, that which is pervaded by the divisions of the Kalpas, and Mahāvāruṇa as well. || 71 ||
The Devyāmata, the Vāyavya, that which is known as the Śivaśāsana, the Śivaśekhara, and the Candrajñāna—these are the fourteen [Tantras]. (72)
The four-faced, the *miyoga*, the *saṃstobha*, the *pratibiṃbaka*, the *arthālaṅkāra*, the *aiśāna*, the *tauṭika*, and the *niṭīraka*. (73)
The one called Kuṭṭima, Tulāyoga, and Tulāpratyaya;
Mahāvidyā, Mahāsaura, Nairṛta, and Paṭṭaśekhara. (74)
Fifteen divisions of the Mukhabimba-tantra have been proclaimed:
Varāha, Pāśabandha, and Piṅgalāmata; || 75 ||
The Dhanurdhara, the Daṇḍadhara, the Śivajñāna, as well as the Aṅkuśa, the Vijñāna, the Āyurveda, and that which is known as the Śrīkālajñāna. (76)
The science of archery (dhanurveda), armor that pierces all fangs,
and Bharata— the treatise on song and instrumental music— these sixteen are traditionally remembered as being [revealed] during the Prodgīta period.
(From PDF 11, p.
655) There are three varieties of *lalita*: *lalita*, *lalitottara*, and then *kaumāra*; furthermore, there are the divisions of *śāla* and that called *sārottarā*. || 78 ||
That which is known as Auśānottara and the Śaśimaṇḍala—these four divisions of the Siddhatantra have been proclaimed. || 79 ||
Liṅgādhyakṣa, Surādhyakṣa, Śaṅkara, and Amareśvara;
at Asaṅkhya there is Aniladvandva, and at Santāna there are seven divisions.
The divine Śivadharmottara, the Īśāna, the Vāyuprokta, and the one called Kuberākhya—these five are recorded as the works spoken by Śarva. (81)
The Haṃsa, the Padma, the Mātaṅga, the Sāmānya, the Yakṣiṇī, the Puṣkara, and the Suprayoga— thus there are seven [forms] of the Supreme Lord.
Gāruḍha, Naiṛta, Raukṣa, Mānya, Buddha, Bhānuka, Prabuddha, Henuka, and Kāla— these nine are proclaimed in the Kiraṇa.
And that which is known as Vātulottara, the Vātula, and the Prarohita;
likewise, the entire Kālajñāna, which is eternal and accomplishes all aims. || 84 ||
The supreme, great-faced, pure, universal, and likewise the soul of the universe—these twelve divisions are proclaimed in the great tantra known as the Vātula. (85)
Through its subdivisions, it is said to be two hundred and seven in number;
those beginning with Kāmika and ending with Ajita have issued from the mouth of Sadyojāta.
The [Tantras] beginning with Dīptā and ending with Suprabhedā originated from the mouth of Vāmadeva;
those beginning with Vijayā and ending with Vīra are the Saṃhitās born from the mouth of Aghora.
From Raurava to Mukhabimba, these [texts] originated from the mouth of Puruṣa;
the eight Saṃhitās beginning with Prodgīta were born from the mouth of Īśāna.
(From *pdf* 12, p.
656) "I shall proclaim the number of the texts; listen in due order, O Maheśvara!
The *Kāmika* is said to consist of a *parārdha*, and the *Yogaja* is said to consist of one hundred thousand [verses]. (89)

Cintya is said to be one hundred thousand, while Kāraṇa is measured at ten million; Ajita is declared to be one hundred thousand times ten thousand (ten million), and Dīpta is called one hundred billion.

The *Sūkṣma* is said to consist of a thousand [verses] equal in number to a lotus; the *Śaṅkha* is measured at one hundred thousand; the *Aṃśumat* consists of five hundred thousand; and the *Suprabheda* consists of thirty million.
Vijaya consists of three crores, while Koṭiniśvāsa is said to consist of ten million; Svāyambhuva is half of three crores, and Anala is thirty thousand.
A *vīra* is said to be a million (*niyuta*), while *raurava* consists of eight hundred thousand (*arbudas*). A *makuṭa* is one hundred thousand, and a *vimala* is three hundred thousand.
The Candrajñāna [Tantra] consists of three thousand [verses], the Mukhabimba of one thousand;
the Prodgīta would consist of three hundred thousand, and the Lalita eight thousand.
The *Sārdhakoṣṭu* is established as six thousand verses;
the *Śarvodgīta* consists of two hundred thousand, and the *Pārameśa* likewise consists of two hundred thousand.
The *Kiraṇa* consists of five crores and the *Vātula* of one hundred thousand;
O Maheśvara, I shall now briefly proclaim the *Tantramūrti*.
The pair of feet is Kāmika, and the ankles are indeed Yogaja;
the toes of the feet are said to be Cintya, while the pair of shanks is Kāraṇa.
The region of the knees should be invincible, the region of the base radiant,
the secret seed subtle, and the surface of the hips a thousandfold.
The back portion should be the *aṃśuka*, the navel should be the *suprabhedaka*, the region of the belly should be the *vijaya*, and the heart should be the *niśvāsa*. || 99 ||
The pair of breasts is called Svāyambhuva, the burning eye is called Vīra, the region of the ears is Vīra, and the two ears are Raurava. (100) [Source: PDF 13, p. 657]
The *Makuṭa* is the crown-tantra, as are the *Aṅga* and *Pratyaṅga*; the *Vimala* is proclaimed to be the extensive [tantra], while the *Candrajñāna* is the site of the *Muṣṭi*. (101)
The face-image is the mouth, which is said to be sung forth by the tongue;
the cheek is called the graceful one, and the forehead is indeed the perfected one. 102.
One should know the *kuṇḍala* as the lineage (*santāna*), the *upavītaka* as that spoken by Śarva,
the *hāra* as the Pārameśa, and the *kiraṇa* as the jewel-ornament.
Likewise, from the navel comes the Kālottara; the wind becomes twenty-two-fold.
Vātula is declared to be the garment, and Śiva-dharma is the ointment.
Having offered the Bimba flower, garlands, and the Siddhānta,
one should worship the God facing south with a body consisting of the Tantra.
For the sake of accomplishment, the Guru should constantly meditate upon Śiva— the form of bliss, stainless, partless, and dancing— especially at the time of the twilight rituals.
The descent of the Rāva Siddhānta Tantras has been presented here;
others are not mentioned for fear of excessive prolixity in this work. (107)
One should not perform any rite from the initial plowing up to the final consecration at the root [of the tree];
if it is performed, the performer and the patron will perish due to the resulting fracture.
Sacrifice alone has been proclaimed in its specific subdivisions,
including the primary rites such as consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and others, which are said to number sixty-six in the forest [tradition].

Whatever ritual procedure, beginning with the plowing and ending with the worship, has been commenced by means of a particular tantra, all of that must be performed by means of that very tantra; one should not perform it according to another tantra.
(From PDF 14, p.
658) The teacher should incorporate what has not been stated [in one] from another tantra;
the plowing and other rites commenced according to the Śivasiddhānta-tantra [are to be followed]. 111.
One should not perform [the ritual] according to another scripture; for if one should do so, there is a confusion of tantras.
Through the fault of such confusion of tantras, the king and the kingdom perish. 112.
A follower of Śiva (Śaiva) may be authorized for everything, both in his own [tradition] and in others;
whereas for others, authority regarding knowledge and reality exists only through their own respective systems.
Thus ends the first chapter, "The Introduction to the Tantra," in the Makuta-tantra.
(From PDF 15, p.
659) The procedure for bathing and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

I shall now describe the procedure for the worship of Śiva; the worship of Śiva is meritorious, auspicious, the bestower of all perfections, the destroyer of the faults that cause great calamities, and the granter of all sovereignty. || 1 ||
Worship is said to be of two kinds: for one's own sake and for the sake of others;
[it is performed] in the body of the Guru, in an auspicious image, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and in one's own self.
Sacrifice for one's own sake is prescribed for a momentary mandala, in water, or for a linga fashioned according to the rules by gods or eminent sages. (3)
A self-manifested linga and an image whose essence is Īśvara are declared to be for the sake of others; they yield the fruit for all individual souls.
In the initiation of the four castes, the Brāhmaṇa is specifically the preceptor;
the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, once initiated, are those who enter [the lineage]. || 5 ||
One should perform sacrifice for one's own sake, but not for the sake of others;
however, by an Ūrdhvaśaiva, it should be performed both for one's own sake and for the sake of others.
These are called the Ūrdhvaśaivas; such a Śaiva Brāhmaṇa is the Guru for those initiated into Nirvāṇa, both for his own sake and for the sake of others.
For among the Śaiva Āgamas, this is the supreme consecration;
it is known as the Makuṭa, the highest, which proclaims the Supreme Tāṇḍava.
In that [state], the auspicious mantra which is superior to the *nāda* consists of the nature beyond sound (*nādātīta*).
For those of the lowest caste, it is employed for initiation and for the purpose of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
Having meditated upon Śiva at dawn and having dedicated all his actions to Śiva,
he should discharge excrement and other waste in the northeast direction of the village.
[One should avoid digging] from a cattle-pen, a dwelling of a deity, an anthill, a reservoir of water, and from the vicinity of Brahmins, cows, men, and women. (11)
Having wrapped his head and remaining silent, facing north, he should make a sound when discharging excrement;
however, for the emission of semen, he should insert his hand into the penis. (12)
Having taken hold of his right hand and performed purification according to the rules in a river, a pond, or a well, he should enter the water.

One should perform the cleansing of the teeth with [twigs from] the Plakṣa, Udumbara, Nimba, and other such trees; one should effect the purification of the nose, mouth, and teeth with the Astra-mantra. (14)

Having recited the *triyaṣṭākṣara* mantra once immediately after purifying the tongue, and having first performed the bath for removing impurities, listen now to the procedure for the mantra-bath (*mantrasnāna*). || 15 ||
Five types of ablutions have been declared for the purification of those who are initiated:
the watery, the fiery, the divine, the aerial, and likewise the mental.
The bath with water is Vāruṇa; that with ashes is Āgneya;
that with rain from a divine cloud is Sādhyā; and that with the dust of cows is Vāyavya. || 17 ||
It is said that bathing with mantras pertains to the mind; thus, there are five kinds of baths:
in a river, or a pond, or a well, or water from a sacred ford (tīrtha). (18)
One should know that water, whether pure or impure, which is near a temple of Śiva, becomes a Śivaliṅga by being sprinkled at the feet of Śiva. (19)
Having bowed to one of them, he should especially perform his bath;
he should prepare a square mandala measuring one cubit.
The practitioner should take the clay with the Astra mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*;
he should place it there with the Sadyojāta mantra and purify it with the Vāmadeva mantra. || 21 ||
Having touched the clay with the Aghora mantra, one should divide it into three parts with the Nara mantra:
first to the east, then to the south, and likewise to the north.
One should consecrate each *rākā* with the *Īśāna* mantra;
having recited the six-limbed *brahman*, one should then assign them in sequence starting from the east. (17.23)
One should scatter portions of earth consecrated with the Astra mantra in the directions where the bites occurred;
one should cast a mass of freshly dug earth into the middle of the sacred bathing site (tīrtha).
One should join it with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, using the root mantra;
having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the sixteen syllables, one should write [the name] beginning with one's own name.
Having recited the Astra mantra, one should perform the mudrā that delivers one from saṃsāra;
by this, there shall be the eradication of even the subtle defects present in the water.
The head, face, heart, private parts, and right foot should be established with lumps of clay as before, and one should smear all the limbs.
Having placed a lump of clay in the north, one should cast it into the middle of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Now hear in due order about the Brahma-fire, the Pitṛs, the Devas, the Ṛṣis, and the Tīrthas. || 28 ||
The external [element] is at the base of the thumb;

Having placed a lotus, a palāśa leaf, tulasī, apāmārga, the tip of a kuśa blade, and jasmine there, one should take them up in excellent vessels.

The Guru should gradually sprinkle all the limbs with the *sadyojāta* mantra;
this ritual bath with water, enveloped by these mantras, is the most supreme and excellent.
Having discarded his previous garment, he should take up a clean cloth;
having thoroughly cleansed his hands and feet, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) once again.
One should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and thereby become purified of all actions;
one should make a sectarian sign on the body with sandalwood mixed with ashes.
For initiated twice-born men, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be six finger-breadths wide;
now listen as the characteristics of the triple mark for the uninitiated are described.
For Brahmins it is said to be six finger-breadths, for kings four finger-breadths,
for Vaiśyas two finger-breadths, and for Śūdras one finger-breadth.
For all others as well, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be like that of a Śūdra;

667) One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) according to the rules; hear now the locations, measurements, and sequence:

On the head and the forehead, on the neck as well as the ears, on the chest and the arms, on the navel and likewise on the back; (92)
One should sequentially place [the mantras] upon the thighs, the knees, and the feet;

The god who causes destruction resides in the ears; Sūrya and Soma reside in the eyes;

Goddess Durgā should be at the navel, and likewise the ancestors on the back;

Then, one should place the three syllables in the triangle, starting from the upper corner and proceeding in order;
having thus meditated upon [the deity] in the form of syllables, facing toward the south.
At its conclusion, one should fashion the foot-imprint and the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā). One should meditate upon the deity with the mind; now hear the procedure for worship with the hands.
Having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (kara-nyāsa), one should carry out all rites;
having first formed the Brahma-mudrā, one should purify [the elements] with the seed-syllable of fire.
One should purify the back and the two hands with the Astra-mantra;
one should then sequentially assign Īśāna and the other deities to the fingers from the thumb to the little finger.
One should sequentially place the six limbs, beginning with the little finger and ending with the thumb;
then, with both hands, one should bind the mantra-mudrā and the Great Sound (mahānāda).
The placement beginning with *sadyojāta* and ending with the little finger is called the *saṃhāra-nyāsa*;
the placement beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger is called the *ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*. || 206 ||
For householders, the placement of creation (sṛṣṭinyāsa) is prescribed for the celibate student;
for forest-dwellers and ascetics, the placement of dissolution (saṃhāranyāsa) is taught. || 207 ||
One should then sequentially assign the limbs of Śiva, beginning with the center and ending with the index finger;
thereafter, one should perform the assignment for the forest-dweller according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Afterwards, one should assign the eight Lords of Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśvaras) in sequence starting from the thumb;
one should assign [the letters] from *a* to *kṣa* in sequence starting from the thumb. (209)
Thereafter, one should install the Prāsāda [mantra] upon the fingers and their joints;
having installed the Mūlaprakṛti [mantras], one should then install them as previously described.
Having applied an ointment of sandalwood and adorned [the image] with fragrant flowers,
one should recite the Śiva-mantra once and bind the Brahma-mudrā.
Having recollected the root seed-syllable and having written down the form of the letter, one should touch all parts of the body, beginning with the head, with both hands while reciting the mantra.
One should perform the placement (vinyāsa) of the phoneme-mantra (varṇamantra), the digit-mantra (kalāmantra), and the aggregate-mantra (piṇḍamantra).
O Maheśvara, listen now specifically to the phoneme-mantra in this manner.

Uttering the letters beginning with *śa* and ending with *sa*, then those from *ba* down to the end of the earth (*p*), then up to the end of the *ca*-group starting from the third letter, and finally ending with *va*. (214)

One should utter, in due order, the series beginning with the sixteenth vowel (Ū) and ending with the moon (A), starting from the first consonant group and ending with Ha, Ka, and Sa respectively. 215.
The seed-syllables of Brahmā ending with the visarga, and the fifth Brahmā-seed-syllable joined with bindu and nāda—this is the auspicious syllable-mantra (varṇamantra). || 216 ||
Thus indeed is the mantra of the phonemes; now hear the sequence for the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa):
one should place the letter *a* on the head and the letter *ā* on the forehead. (217)
The letter *ī* is in the right eye, the letter *ī* is in the left eye;
the letter *u* is in the right nostril, and the letter *ū* is in the left nostril.
The syllable *ṛ* on the right ear, the syllable *ṝ* on the left ear;
the syllable *ḷ* on the right cheek, and the syllable *ḹ* on the left cheek. (219)
(From PDF 35, p.
679) The letter *e* should be on the upper lip, and likewise the letter *ai* on the lower lip;
the letter *o* is on the upper teeth, while the letter *au* is on the lower teeth. (220)
The syllable *aṃ* is in the middle of the palate, while the syllable *aḥ* is at the top of the palate;
the *ka*-group is on the right hand, and the *ca*-group is on the left hand.
The *ṭa*-group [of consonants] shone on his right foot, and the *ta*-group on his left foot;
likewise, the sixth group [the *ṣa*-group] was on his right side and the seventh [the *sa*-group] on his left side.
One should place the syllable *ma* at the region of the navel and the syllable *ya* on the skin;
the syllable *ra* at the region of the blood and the syllable *la* at the region of the flesh.
One should place the syllable *va* in the region of the fat, the syllable *śa* in the region of the sinews,
the syllable *kṣa* in the region of the marrow, and the syllable *sa* in the region of the semen.
The letter *ha* is said to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*); one should place it between the eyebrows.
One should place the letter *ka* at the region of the penis and the letter *kṣa* on the testicles. (225)
Now, hear the sequence for the ritual placement of the *kalās* as prescribed by the order of the scriptures:
having uttered the twelfth seed-syllable (*bīja*), one should then recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). (226)
Recalling the five Brahmans in their proper sequence, one should contemplate the Kalā-mantras;
O Maheśvara, listen as I describe the form of the five Brahmans.
Resembling pure crystal, with four faces and four arms,
radiant with ornaments such as necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and earrings.
He wears a crown of cowries and a white sacred thread;
he is equipped with a shield and a chisel, and his hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having the nature of Sadyojāta, with a radiant luster like the moon;
originating from Vāmadeva, he is red in color, four-faced, and four-armed.
His belly is adorned with a girdle and a waist-belt resplendent with tinkling anklets; likewise, he wears a crown of coral and a golden sacred thread. (231)
His lotus-like hands are joined with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding a noose and a goad;
he has three eyes, possesses the three-fold grace, and is adorned with earrings. || 232 ||
This indeed is the essential nature of Vāmadeva as the embodiment of mantra;
it is Aghora, terrifying to those with fangs, and possesses a luster like crushed collyrium. (233)
He has eight arms, three eyes, and four faces, and wears matted locks;
he is clad in red garments and has a red upper cloth.
With his limbs smeared with red sandalwood and adorned with a red garland,
he holds in his right hands a trident, a vetāla, a sword, and a discus.
With his left hands, he holds a serpent, spittle, a bell, and a gesture of astonishment;
likewise, he wears a blue ring and a sacred thread made of a serpent.
And thus, having invoked the Aghora mantra, one should meditate on the Puruṣa, whose nature is the form of the mantra,
appearing like saffron in color, with four faces and four arms.
Holding a chisel, a trident, a hand-drum, and a mace in his right and left hands,
he has a triangular face that is gentle and slightly smiling.
A golden ring, a golden upper garment, a crown of pearls, and a ruby finger-ring. || 239 ||
This is the essential nature of the mantra-form of the Puruṣa-mantra:
ten-armed, three-eyed, five-faced, and wearing matted hair.
He holds a vajra, a trident, a staff, a sword, and the gesture of fearlessness in his right hands, and he holds a noose, a goad, and a hand-drum in his left hands.
The ruby crown and the ruby finger-ornament are gentle,
possessing the luster of crystal, and having the very form of the embodiment of Īśa. (242)
The form of Aghora is indeed fierce, while the remaining forms are declared to be gentle;
that gentle form, which is the nature of Brahman, is the supreme cause of creation.
The male organ is indeed that of Īśvara, bestowing lordship;
the left [organ] belongs to Viṣṇu, which is most excellent and the very cause of maintenance.
Aghora is said to be the form of Rudra, the cause of dissolution;
likewise, Sadāśiva and Īśāna bestow the great liberation. || 245 ||
Thus [ends the section on] Brahmā as the presiding deity; now hear the procedure for the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Kalās.
The Kalās are supreme, consisting of the deities, and the mantra of the Kalās is tantric.
One should install the power of the *kalās* (parts) together with the right [hand], using the *kalās* as the forms of Brahmā; the *śaktis*, however, have the form of maidens. || 247 ||
Their lotus-like hands are adorned with the goad, the noose, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness;
they are complete with all ornaments and graced by crowns.
The kalās of Īśāna are five; those of Puruṣa are four;
the kalās of Aghora are eight; and those of Vāmadeva are thirteen.
The unborn [deity] has thirty-eight parts (kalās); these are considered the thirty-eight parts.
I shall now describe the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the power of the parts (kalā-śakti) by means of those parts; listen to it in due order. || 250 ||
One should duly assign these five digits (kalās) in sequence: Śaśinī, Tvaṅgadā, as well as iṣṭā, Marīcikā, and Jvālinī.
First the south, then the north, then the west, as well as above and the northeast; one should thus assign the positions in these five directions.
(From PDF 38, p.
682) Śānti, Vidyā, and Pratiṣṭhā are the four constituent parts of Pradhāna.
One should assign these, along with Puruṣa and Śakti, to the four faces. (253)
The east, the south, the north, and the west—these are Diti, Ghaṭā, Kṣayā, and Niṣṭhā; likewise, Karma and Ādi arise from fever.
One should assign these digits (kalās) of Aghora to the heart and other parts:
specifically to the heart, the throat, and likewise to the pair of shoulders. (255)
In the abdomen, in the navel, and likewise in the posterior part, as well as in the chest—these eight locations will be described in their proper order. (256)
Rajārakṣā, Ratī, Pālikā, Saṃyamā, Vṛddhi, Kriyādhātrī, and again Bhrāmaṇī should be fashioned. (257)
Mohinī and Bhayā on the left—these are the thirteen kalās;
[they are located] in the penis, the anus, the two thighs, the two knees, and the two shanks. || 258 ||
Afterwards, one should place [the goddesses] in order upon the two buttocks, the waist, and the two sides:
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dhṛti, Lakṣmī, and likewise Medhā. (259)
One should place these digits— Kānti, Svadhā, Dhṛti, Ābhā, and Sadyojāta— on the two feet, the two hands, the two forearms, and the two armpits.
Having meditated upon the form consisting of Śiva, which comprises thirty-eight kalās,
one should then place the piṇḍa-mantras in their respective locations.
Having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face;
having placed Aghora on the heart, one should assign Vāmadeva to the private parts.
One should place the unborn [syllable] at the feet of the other, and then assign the limbs;
having assigned the heart to the heart, one should assign the crest-lock (śikhā) to the head.
Having assigned *Śivāya* to the crest (*śikhā*), one should assign the armor (*kavaca*) to the two breasts;
with the eye-mantra (*netramantra*), the binding of the ten directions (*daśadigbandhana*) is prescribed for the eyes. (39.264)
One should sequentially place the seed-syllables of the five Brahmans and the six limbs;
however, in the group of sky-seed syllables, one should exclude the six syllables.
The first is declared to be Ajāta; the third is called Vāma; Aghora is declared to be the fifth; Narasiṃha shall be the eleventh. || 266 ||
The thirteen-syllable Īśāna is declared to be the seed-syllable of Brahmā;
the second is said to be the heart, while the fourth shall be the head.
They know the sixth syllable to be the crest-mantra (śikhā), the twelfth to be the armor (kavaca),
the fifteenth is declared to be the eye (netra), and likewise the sixteenth to be the weapon (astra).
Accompanied by the utterances *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*, one should also perform this six-limbed placement (*nyāsa*) for the purpose of protecting the limbs. (269)
O Maheśvara, hear now the colors of the six-limbed deities:
white, yellow, red, black, lightning-colored, and saffron.
Four-armed and three-eyed, endowed with the gesture of granting boons,
he holds in his hands a skull-bowl, a trident, the boon-granting mudrā, and an axe.
The *astra* and *netra* [mudrās] are indeed *raudra*, while the remaining ones are remembered as *saumya*.
One should offer perfume, flowers, and incense with the *varṇa-mantra*.

Having meditated upon the essential nature, one should worship it; immediately thereafter, one should recite the *piṇḍa-mantra* as the *jñānamudrā*. Afterward, listen to the cause of the seed-syllables (*bīja*). || 273 ||
The semi-vowels ending with *vīra-bīja* (the letter *m*), together with the nasal (*nāda*) as the sixteenth mora—this auspicious *piṇḍa-mantra* is the mantra that embodies all mantras. || 274 ||
(From PDF 40, p.

684) Having recited [the mantra] once and meditated upon Śiva, one should bind the seal of knowledge (jñānamudrā). I shall now describe the sequence for the different types of liṅgas, along with their specific details in due order. || 275 ||
The two types of lingas are said to be the mobile and the immobile;
one should always worship the Supreme Lord in the mobile linga. || 276 ||
The stationary *liṅga* deity, however, is preceded by the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the mantra;
but a *liṅga* devoid of the mantra-consecration is merely a physical form. (277)
The mobile liṅga is indeed the specific form; Maheśvara is the divine Guru.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always worship him in the form of one's own master. || 278 ||
One should meditate on that which is called *sādākhya*, which possesses both aspects of karma;
for the true reality is the essential nature of the supreme *sādākhya*. || 279 ||
O Maheśvara, having abandoned his previous form, Sadāśiva— the pure one who possesses the form of all deities— assumes the very form known as Sādākhya.
Above that, one should place the form of Nṛtta for Sādākhya;
having meditated upon the form of Nṛtta as eternal, beginning with the Southern Abode (Dakṣiṇālaya).
The supreme abode, consisting of the nine principles, which brings about all prosperity, is the form of light, eternally manifesting as the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution. (282)
He has four arms, is ever-naked, and is without beginning or end; he possesses a cause, is auspicious, the supreme nirvāṇa, the body of all, and the eternal Śiva. (283)

Having meditated upon his form as the Sādākhya, one should place Naṭeśvara in the center; established within the middle of the heart-lotus, he consists of the Nāda-tantra and is composed of the Kalās.
One should constantly meditate upon Maheśvara as having one face, four arms, and two feet, with a rounded waist, either seated or performing a beautiful dance. 285.
(From PDF 41, p.
685) It has five faces, ten arms, and two feet; it is circular in the middle, the size of a thumb, immovable, the pure reality, and consists of nine aspects. (286)
The self, however, consists of the letter *sa*; the inner self, moreover, consists of the *bindu*. || 287 ||
The Supreme Self, residing in the seed-syllable of space, is the Nāda consisting of sixteen tantric elements;
having worshipped everything in due order with the Heart-mantra, [one should proceed]. (288)
The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight parts is considered to consist of thirty-eight aspects;
it is the supreme dance of the thirty-eight. Listen now to the sequence of the timing for this placement.
The entire sequence [of worship] is performed with the heart-mantra;
it consists of thirty-eight self-mantras. || 290 ||
Listen to the sequence of the thirty-eight supreme dances and their placement;
[I shall explain] the purification of the body, the placement of the *kalās*, and the mantra consisting of thirty-eight parts. (291)
One should place Yoga, Nṛtta, and Mantra in their respective positions in due order.
The sequence for the purification of the self has been declared; now hear the sequence for the purification of the site.
One should dig the ground to the depth of one cubit and fill it back up gradually with that same earth.
Having made the surface of the ground level, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
It should be provided with a canopy and a banner, and furnished with plantain trees and areca palms.
It was joined with a garland of *darbha* grass, adorned with strings of pearls, strewn with flower garlands, and embellished with rows of lamps. || 295 ||
Served by many *pālikās* in the ten directions. (p.
686) [page missing]
Having filled [the vessel] with pure water, one should perform the placement of the sun (sauranyāsa). || 307 ||
Uttering the seed-syllable of fire (ra) ending with the visarga, followed by "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should purify the ground, the back [of the hands], and the right and left hands.
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe in sequence the root mantra and the six limbs:
the Praṇava joined with fire (Ra), followed by the letter at the end of the group ending in Ka (Sa). (309)

That [syllable] with the nasal drop (bindu) and the long vowel at its root, joined again with its head, preceded by space (vyoma), ending with the visarga, and concluding with "namaḥ," is the mantra of the Sun. || 310 ||
One should place the heart-mantra, which is joined with the peaceful *bindu*, upon the heart;
having placed [the mantra] for the sun upon the head, one should place the *bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ* upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*).

Having performed the placement of the armor (*kavaca*) on the earth with the mantra "trivedina," one should place the solar weapon (*saurāstra*), which consists of the fire-seed (*agnibīja*) ending in the visarga, conjoined with the directions.
One should worship the imperishable Śiva, conjoined with the beloved Bindu;
having uttered the single [syllable] without Bindu, one should utter it ending with the *polka* and the Sun.
With this mantra, one should cause the offering of incense and flowers;
with kusha grass and water, one should worship the sacrificial post (yūpa) up to its end with red sandalwood.
Having established a single *arghya* offering, listen to the sequence for the meditation on the Sun:
he has one face, two arms, and two eyes, and holds a lotus smeared with ghee. (315)
Standing in the midst of a circle of light, brilliantly radiant and clad in red garments, he is endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament. (316)
O Maheśvara, one should meditate upon my form as the Great Soul, red in color, having four faces and eight arms, like the lord of the day (the sun). || 317 ||
Three-eyed and four-armed, the preventer of ingratitude,
mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven horses, he is the illuminator who radiates light.
(From PDF 43, p.
688) He is joined with Uṣas and united with Varuṇa; he is endowed with radiance and the twilight, joined with Medhā and Prajñā, and accompanied by the planets beginning with Soma. || 319 ||
The Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—these planets, in this order, are the destroyers of death. || 320 ||
The charcoal of Soma is the color of cow’s milk; that of Aṅgāra is red in color;
that of Budha is said to be dark green; and that of Bṛhaspati is blue in color. || 321 ||
Venus is the color of jasmine and the moon; Saturn is black in color;
Rāhu resembles a crow or a cloud; and Ketu is said to have the appearance of smoke. (322)
All are seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), endowed with all the auspicious marks (lakṣaṇas), adorned with every ornament, and are proclaimed to have two arms. || 323 ||
One should place Soma in the northern quarter, Bhārgava facing the eastern direction,
Aṅgāraka in the southern quarter, and Bṛhaspati in the west.
One should place Śanaiścara in the northeast, Rāhu in the southeast,
Ketu in the southwest region, and Budha in the northwest.
In front, one should place the chariot and the horses, and Aruṇa in front;
one should also assign Prabhā, Uṣas, Sandhyā, and Prajñā.
One should worship Rodha and Sūryacaṇḍeśa in the northeastern direction;
then one should worship the eight world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective locations. || 327 ||

One should offer all things, such as perfumes, flowers, and so forth, by means of their respective names; likewise, one should cause the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and the water-offering (arghya) to be presented.
The procedure for the worship of the Sun has been declared; now hear the characteristics of the enclosures.
O Maheśvara, listen likewise to the names of the five enclosures.
The inner mandala shall be the first; that within the inner necklace (antarhāra) is the second;
the middle necklace (madhyahāra) shall be the third; and that beginning from the middle is the fourth. (330)
The fifth is proclaimed as the Mahāmaryādika;
now hear the dimensions of these ramparts in their proper order.
The inner necklace (antarmaṇulamāna) should be half the measure of a staff (daṇḍa);
the single inner string (antarhāraka), however, consists of one [staff], while the middle necklace (madhyahāra) consists of two staffs.
The fourth [enclosure] is fourteen cubits from the center and the fifth is seventeen cubits;
this is the location of the well for the guardian of the third enclosure wall.
The place of wealth is proclaimed to be between Indra and Agni;
the clothing hall is said to be between Āgneya and Yāmya.
The place for the couch is said to be between the northwest and the north;
the northeast is called the great pavilion of the great boundary. || 335 ||
According to the wish of the patron, a pavilion (maṇḍapa) may be constructed anywhere; this is called the enclosure-pavilion (prākāramaṇḍapa). Now hear the procedure for the worship of the door.
Then, one should worship the conch, Jaya, situated in the middle of the night;
and on the right side, the staircase which has the luster of jasmine and the moon.
Afterwards, in the center, is Padmanidhi, situated on the northern side; immediately following is Hastivaktra, who has a shell-like neck, grants boons, and is steadfast. (338)
The one named Kṣipraprasāda and the two Vināyakas who create obstacles—
the colors of these ten Vighnas shall now be described individually.
White, red, as well as black, coral, blue, smoky-grey, gold, the rising sun, pearl, and topaz. (340)
On the right door-panel, Brahmā is the presiding deity;
and on the left door-panel, Viṣṇu is said to be the deity. (341)
The Madhyasthā-phalakā [are located there], and Rudra is their presiding deity (adhidevatā).
On the right side of the door-panel, however, the Śikhā has Bhṛṅgīśa as its deity.
The two deities of the door-opening are Dhvani and Ketana;
and for all the lintels (paṭṭikās), the presiding deity is Maheśvara, known as Subrahmaṇya. || 343 ||
For the Phalaka deities, Vāyu is the presiding deity;
having consecrated it with the Astra-mantra, one should then plug the hole.
Reciting the Netra-mantra, one should take up the two bracelets representing the lords of the sun and moon,
as well as the perfume, flowers, incense, lamp, and sacrificial oblation.
The two door-bolts are said to have the Sun and Moon as their presiding deities;
the door-panels, situated in the middle of the door-posts, have the eight mountain deities as their presiding deities.
Eight nāgas are proclaimed as the ornaments of the door-panels;
one should worship the deities residing in the door-panels with their respective names. || 347 ||
One should insert the left hand into the right side of the door-panel;
then, by means of the Vāyu-mantra, one should cause the movement of the mechanisms. || 348 ||
One should worship the deities of all the door-panels in this manner:
to the right of the door-deities are the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas. (349)
Likewise, for the deities of the western gate, there are the goddesses of the God of Gods;
for the deities of the northern gate, there are the six syllables, the syllable Om, and the Vyāhṛtis.
At the fourth natural gate, however, there is obeisance to Agniśavāya;
on the right side, moreover, is the deity named Śivajyotis. (351)
(From PDF 46, p.
691) On the side of the northern gate is the deity named Vijaya, for the sake of the qualities of swift knowledge of the deities of the southern gate. || 352 ||
To the deities of the western gate, and to Bhūta, Rudra, and Ambikā;
to the deities of the northern gate, and to Abhaya and Guṇa. || 353 ||
In the third door of the natural form, one should worship the auspicious deity in front,
and on the right side, one should worship the goddess Vīrabhadra.
On the northern side, however, is the one named Śivajyotiṣin;
and among the deities of the southern gate are the Mārutas, Daityas, and Dānavas.
The deities of the western gate are Suyaśas, Deva, and Vikrama;
the deities of the northern gate are Madhu, Bhūta, Anala, and Rudraka.
In the second enclosure, at the front is the deity Sundara;
on the right side is the deity Nīlalohita of the Pārśva deities. || 357 ||
On the northern side are the deities of Kālabhairava;
on the southern side are the deities of the door, surrounded by Śivānanda.
And for the deities of the western gate, [he should offer] to Sākṣisatyapriya;
and for the deities of the northern gate, to the lords (īśāna) of the divine cities.
First, hear the procedure for the worship of the deities at the doorway of the Prākṛti;
Sarasvatī is at the front of the door, and likewise, the Bull (Vṛṣa) is in front of her.
In front of that, one should worship the ten Vighneśas and the trident;
Nandīśa on the right side and Mahākāla on the left.
In the middle, [one should worship] Danteśvara; below that, Kamalavāsinī;
and among the deities of the southern gate, Daṇḍimuṇḍī, O beautiful one.
At the end of the deities of the western gate, Paśupati shall be;
for the deities of the northern gate, Bhrukuṭī and Vijayabhairava. (363)
One should worship Śrīdevī in the upper part, and then Bhūmidevī below;
one should worship Jñānaśakti and Kriyāśakti at the entrance to the womb.
Having thus performed the worship of the doors, one should thereafter worship the pavilion;
with the mantra beginning "vāstoṣpate," one should worship the deity Vāstu in the northeast.
Having worshipped well with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should strike the great bell;
it indicates that the eight Vasus are the deities of the jewels and Soma is their presiding deity.
One should perform worship at the proper time with the great resonance of bells;
by that great sound, there is the destruction of the Rākṣasas.

The *liṅga* is to be known as fourfold, as enjoined by the scriptures: the stationary (*sthāvara*), the divine (*daivika*), the ṛṣi-related (*ārṣaka*), and likewise the collective (*gāṇava*) and the human (*mānuṣa*). || 368 ||
Now hear the characteristics of these secondary (devikā) liṅgas:
the liṅga shall be elongated in shape, arising from depressions and elevations.
Joined with lines, dots, and rasas, elevated by the faces like a stream, having the form of a mountain peak, with a wide opening at the top and endowed with a crest. 370.
With the two hands joined in the shape of a casket (saṃpuṭa) and devoid of the sacred thread (brahmasūtra)—endowed with these characteristics, it is called a divine (devika) liṅga. || 371 ||
The base of the liṅga should be thick, and likewise its top;
the middle of the liṅgas should also be thick, having the shape of a coconut fruit. || 372 ||
Resembling the fruit of the plantain tree, with the shape of the fruit of the *bilva* tree, possessing two broad and protruding breasts, and having limbs resting upon jars. (373)

It is gross, and it is neither too thin nor too thick.
To the Supreme Śiva, [I offer] the face that is both partless and with parts, whose meaning is partless, formidable and frowning,
yet gentle, disheveled, fiercely valorous, and bearing the auspicious marks.

The *komaka*, the *vīravipula*, the eternal *droṇabhadra*, the *casureśa*, and the purifying; likewise the *nimnonnata* and the *nissargabheṣaja*; and the *vyākhyātavīra* and the *subhadraliṅga*. || 385 ||

The Lord [perceived] the distorted white [substance], the binding with a trident, the pillar, the blessing, and the sun-like; the purified, the water-sprinkling, and the sprinkling of *vivilava*, *vaikrānta*, and *kuśa* grass. 386.
And that which is heated by acquisition, among the barley-grasses; five and five middling [ants];
the side-tip, the root-tip, the excellent middle-tip, the upper-tip-mark, and the square-mark. || 387 ||
He spoke of the *avādita* with its long and rounded mark, the one consisting of lotuses, and the five-fold auspicious *kuṣṭha*;
also the *manda*, the *kaiḍa*, the *cakara*, the *subhru*, the *vilambita*, and the golden *suvarṇa-liṅga*.
One should purify the *liṅga-pīṭha* and the site itself with water from the heart-mantra. (50, p. 697) [409]
Having worshipped the entire body of the *liṅga* with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting [the appropriate mantras],
one should touch the region of the *liṅga*s head with the *Īśāna* mantra.
One should touch the face region of the *liṅga* with the *tatpuruṣa* [mantra], and one should touch both sides of the *liṅga* with the two arms using the *aghora* [mantra]. (411)
One should touch the back of the *liṅga* with the Vāmadeva mantra;
one should touch the feet as far as the pedestal with both arms using the Sadyojāta mantra. (412)
One should worship the limbs of the Goddess from the great fillet (mahāpaṭṭikā) down to the edge of the sandals;
the temple of the Goddess and its own limbs is called her "liṅga," which I shall now describe. || 413 ||
Prāsāda, sadana, sadma, gṛha, dhāman, niketana,
vimāna, harmya, vāsa, mandira, and ālaya are synonyms for a house or palace.
And "nilaya" are likewise renowned as synonyms for it.
O Maheśvara, listen as I describe the characteristics of the celestial chariot (vimāna). || 415 ||
The first is the foundation (adhiṣṭhāna), the second is the plinth (upāna), the third is the terrace (jagatī), and the fourth is the lotus (padma). || 416 ||
The fifth is Kumuda, and likewise the sixth is Paṭṭikā;
the seventh is declared to be Bhinna, and the eighth is the pillar (stambha). || 417 ||
The ninth is the Pālikā, the tenth is the Kampā, the eleventh is the Kapotā, and the twelfth is the Bhūtamālikā. || 418 ||
The thirteenth is the neck, while the nose is the fourteenth;
the fifteenth is the pinnacle, and the top of the stūpa becomes the sixteenth.
And there is a sixteenth part of the powers; hear their names in sequence:
the first is Ādhāraśakti, and the second is Śaktikā.

The third is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), the fourth is the wheel of light (*jyotiścakra*), the fifth is the power of qualities (*guṇa-śakti*), and the sixth is the power of location (*sthāna-śaktikā*). (421)
The thirteenth is Jñānaśakti; the fourteenth belongs to Arbhavīya;
the fifteenth is Kalyāṇī; and Maheśvarī is at the tip of the stūpa. 422.
One should sequentially place these powers, beginning with the *adhiṣṭhāna* and ending with the *sthūpī*.
Thus, listen as the characteristic of the abode of the ritual act (*kṛti*) through power (*śakti*) is described. || 423 ||
That which is accumulated and that which is not accumulated is called "collected" (*upasañcita*).
That which is joined with heaps of stones is "accumulated," while that which lacks a solid base is "not accumulated. (424)
Equipped with its primary and secondary limbs, it is called the "accumulated" (upasañcita).
Now hear, in due order, the names of the vimānas and the liṅgas and śaktis. || 425 ||
The celestial vehicle (vimāna) shall be known as Nālikā, and the liṅga should have equal sections;
[the powers] are Kṣānti, Śakti, Pralīkā, Āsthāpanā, and Jayātmikā.
The Svastika-liṅga is established as the four-faced Prajāśakti;
the Pratiṣṭhā-liṅga is Vārāhī, auspicious and beneficial in every respect. || 427 ||
The female organ is the Liṅga of Action-power; the back of the hand is Gaṇādhipa;
the smoke-colored Śakti is brilliantly blazing; and the well-formed Liṅga is the expanded hood.

The Śrīcchanda is said to have twenty fingers as its measure; it is called the power of the fruit-bearing one (phalinī-śakti), auspicious through the movement of the powers of the qualities (guṇa-śakti-vṛtta-bhadra), and it is the fruit-liṅga (phala-liṅga) that is to be attained. 429.
The Śrīkānta Liṅga is established, conjoined with the Bhrāmaṇī Śakti;
the abode known as Śrīpratiṣṭhā is indeed the Mūlasthūla Liṅga.
The power of the self (ātma-śakti) is milk; the gross linga is situated in the middle.
The power of the mantra (mantra-śakti) is the severing of the head; the face is the partless linga (niṣkala-liṅga). || 431 ||
The protective enclosure of the limbs (*rakṣāraṅgopuṭa*) is indeed the *liṅga* named *sakala*.
It is called the power of the armlets (*aṅgadāśakti*), the giver of all, and it signifies the meaning of the *niṣka* [necklace]. (51.432)
The protective enclosure (rakṣāraṃ) and the gateway (gopura) are indeed the Liṅga named Sakala;
it is called Aṅgāraśakti, while that which bestows all [blessings] is the Niṣkala.
The power of action (karaṇa-śakti) is said to be Viṣṇucchadana and Harmyaka;
the power of agency (kriyā-śakti) consists of Bhadrā, Ṭaṅka, Liṅka, and Svadhāmayī.
The Kailāsa Liṅga is formidable, conjoined with the power (śakti) of Pārvatī;
and the Candra-makuṭa Liṅga is likewise endowed with Śakti and Śaktimān. || 434 ||
The seat is the Rudra-metre, and Bhairavī is the Kaliṅga;
the scattered liṅga is the Vṛkita, and the Arāma-metre belongs to you.
Caṇḍiliṅga, Viṭā, Śakti, Śrīkūṭa, Kāntaliṅgaka, Nādaśakti, Kumbha, Bhadraliṅga, and Rajāyinī. (436)
The supreme Liṅga is the limb of victory, endowed with the power of play;
it is the celestial chariot of the Śiva-liṅga, adorned with the stainless power of forbearance.
They call the soft linga "Endowed with the Primordial Power" (Ādiśaktisamāyuta);
the Haṃsa-chanda is the "Abode," and the Vīra is the "Vipula-lingaka. (438)
The power of delusion, the bull-bannered one, the phallus of Śāligrāma, the object of wandering;
the poison, the abode of sandalwood, the crooked and auspicious laughter. || 439 ||
Padmāṅgasadana, Sthiraliṅga, and Manonmanī are said to be the purifying liṅgas of the Padmabhadra vimāna.
The *ṛddhi* type has a sacrificial seat (*savana*) that is uneven with prominent and depressed areas;
the *rudraśakti* type has a dwelling (*sadana*); the *kukkuṭa* type has a phallus (*liṅga*) resembling a peacock. || 441 ||
(From PDF 52, p. 700):
Paraśakti is known as Nikānta, and Liṅgapālinī;
Rudrakānta is the abode, while Raviliṅga is the Grāmaṇī. 442.
The auspicious Liṅga with splendor belongs to the Vimāna of Yogabhadra;
the abode of Bhogacchanda is Śoṣaṇī, which pertains to the Cakraliṅga.
The Vindhyacakra is the celestial chariot (vimāna), while the Śṛṅgaliṅga is most terrifying;
the Merukūṭa is the celestial chariot, and the Bandhaliṅga is the limb of power (śakti).
The abode of Śrī Mahendra is the southern Staṃbhaliṅga;
it is called Kalyāṇaśakti, and Budbuda is the Rāśiliṅgaka.

It is said that the power presiding over desire (kāmadhiśakti) is the Śrī-maṇḍala, which has a stone liṅga; while the power of thought (cintyeśakti), known as Saumya, is the maṇḍala with a painted liṅga.
The power called Paiśāca is said to be victorious and auspiciously illuminating;
the power called Pālinī is said to be characterized by the auspicious liṅga.
The abode of Viṣṇu’s power, however, possesses the luster of a blue mountain; it is merged with the power of light and is characterized by excellent lingas. || 448 ||
The supreme power, the sound *sisū*, is established as the *prabhu-liṅga*;
and the *vijaya-liṅga* is conjoined with the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*).
The Lalita [liṅga] is lovely and heated with passion, endowed with the power of resonance;
it is non-dual, situated between restraint and moderation, and possesses the power of the Tāṇḍava dance. || 450 ||
The dwelling named Śrīvilāsa, the Pipīlikasuliṅgaka,
the Atipratiṣṭha, the Śakti, and the Somacchanda mansion.
One should fashion a serpent, adorned with excellent marks and joined with power, upon the stalk; and one should likewise make it circular, situated at the side of the tooth.
(From PDF 53, p.
701) The base, the tip, the liṅga, and the śānti [levels] constitute the central lotus of Indra;
it possesses the lord of the assembly (sannadhī), the śakti, the śrīvatsa, and the head of Ṛta, along with the third śakti. || 453 ||
The abode with a lotus emblem is square and possesses excellent lingas;
it is called Vidrumāśakti, while the one with a trident and linga is known as Prokṣyadāya.
The tenfold power (daśaśakti) is the liṅga that has proceeded from the activity of Kriyā;
likewise, the heart-liṅga (hṛlliṅga) is its exit, and the great power (mahāśakti) is the limb of victory (jayāṅgaka).
The *vilambita* type is the *suliṅga*, while the *viśālabhadra* is the *vaiṇava*; the *liṅga* known as *kāma* is the *bhadraliṅga*. (456)
They call it the Golden Liṅga, which is endowed with the power of craving;
it is the abode of the Gaṇas and Āśālas, possessing the luster of copper. || 457 ||
The *kāmaśakti* is for the throat; the *liṅga-raudraka* is for Maheśa; the *bhadra-liṅga* is for Viṣṇu; and the *śivaliṅga* is for Śiva. (458)
In the hall known as Rudraśaktīti, there is the Śakti of the body of the Candraliṅga;
the abode at Padmāvasāna possesses the Śaktis of the mobile liṅgas and others. || 459 ||
The eternal linga of Dhairya, Bhūtaśakti, and Viṣṇuka;
the sixfold Liṅgakālī, and Vidrumālayagopura. (460)
In the seven streams of the Liṅga, Raviśakti is indeed all-encompassing;
in the nine streams of the excellent Liṅga, Dādhārī is the abode of Lalitā.
The palace of Lakṣmīndra belongs to the Ṣoḍaśādhāra-liṅga;
the vast [palace] of Kāmaśakti belongs to the Sahasra-śubhra-liṅga.
The excellent *liṅga* at the peak of Śikharāgra is the "Siddhi-upplāya-śatraka";
they call it the Māṇikya-liṅga, which destroys anger, poison, kings, and fire. (463)
(From PDF 54, p.
702) The abode of Kṛṣṇāśakti is auspicious, adorned with a garland of moons;
it possesses two stone liṅgas and two gopuras at the front of its double-winged hall. (464)
The flame of the *liṅga* at the tip of the crest [of the hair] fulfills the desire for the consumption of the earth;
the *vāk-śakti* of the *sahasradhārā-liṅga* is the abode of victory. (465)
The hundred-and-eight-fold stream of the Liṅga is the cessation that is the abode of all;
it is the goal of all other purposes, the source of all foundations, and the measure of the abode born of the limbs.
The *yava-liṅga* is the abode of the beauty of the power of delusion (*moha-śakti*);
the *sphaṭika-liṅga* is the true radiance of the power of fortitude (*dhṛti-śakti*). || 467 ||
The temple known as Kṣetraśakti is the Nāgara style, with its mind fixed on the Liṅga; the temple known as Nāgaśakti is the Drāviḍa style, shaped like a rising pinnacle (vardhamānaka).
Patience is the power, the abode is the chariot, and fortitude is the couch;
this abode of the powers of the *liṅga* is established through the individual soul (*jīva*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
His own nature is the refuge of the individual soul, his essential form being that of the dancer in the midst [of the cosmic dance];
therefore, one should worship the Guru, the actor whose form is light, who dwells in the center of the Self of all.
He whose nature consists of both qualities and the absence of qualities, the all-encompassing Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
[is worshipped] with conchs, trumpets, and lutes, with the sounding of bells, and beautiful anklets.
Having been honored by men with a great roar, and remembering Dakṣiṇeśa, one should worship Naṭeśvara, whose abode is situated within the center of the Liṅga. || 472 ||
Therefore, with every effort, having meditated upon its center and having uttered the mantra of the *liṅga*, listen to the extraction of that mantra. || 473 ||
But the fourth of the third [group], endowed with *bindu* and *nāda*, is declared to be the *liṅga-mantra*; it is said to be the station of the powers (*śakti*). (55.474)
The seat known as Ārādhārā is the primordial form of Śakti;
the world-constituent Śakti, however, is Kumuda, which possesses the power of the qualities (guṇa). || 475 ||
The power that protects the fillet is Śakti; the throat is Kalyāṇaśakti;
the lower fillet is Kāmādhī; and the great fillet is Manonmanī.
The upper band is the Great Power (Mahāśakti), and the foundation consists of ten aspects;
the pillar is the power of Sound (Nādaśakti), and the lotus belongs to the power of Bhairava.
The power of the limbs whose roots have blossomed is the power residing in the abode of the lotus;
the power consisting of the pericarp is the power that causes the drying up of the waters. 478.
The throat is indeed Kālaśakti, and Mahānāsī is of the nature of victory;
the elevation of that Mahānāsī is the peak consisting of nine powers.
In its center, O Pārvatī, beneath the stūpa, is a lotus possessing power;
Karṇa is the power of compassion, and the Kumbha is the vessel of nectar.
The upper pitcher is the power of the crest (śikhā-śakti); the Śrīvatsa-mark is the power of sound;
the neck-ring is the power of resonance (nāda-śakti); and the base is the power of the mantra.
The bud of the blue lotus, however, has a subtle power at its tip;
thus, the abode consisting of power is said to have a manifest form.
The Liṅga is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala); indeed, the partless one is of the nature of light.
Standing in the midst of the radiance of that light is the wondrous Southern Naṭa.
The dance of Dakṣiṇeśvara is devoid of qualities, stainless, eternal, the intermediate, the supreme state, higher than the Supreme Power, and Vedic. || 484 ||
(From PDF 56, p.
704) [He is] the immovable one, the bestower of boons, the truth, devoid of cause and illustration, the temple, the Lord of the South and the North, the pure, the primordial Master. (485)
I bow to the Guru who is impartial, established in his fundamental form, the void, possessing the resonance of the void,
consisting of eternal bliss, accompanied by Ambā, the witness, and identical with Sadāśiva.
Everything transcends conceptual construction; it is without inherent nature yet ever-arisen, equal, in a state of uniform flavor, facing all directions and upward. || 487 ||
The Lord of the South is the Great Secret, eternally engaged in wondrous dance;
from the throat upwards, the temple is eight-cornered and melting. (488)
That which is rounded from the neck upwards is praised as the Vesara style;
O Maheśvara, I shall now declare the names of the ninety-six varieties of the three classes [of temples].
The *nalika*, the *pralika*, the *svastika*, the four-faced (*caturmukha*), the *sarvatobhadra*, and the brilliantly radiant *hastipṛṣṭha*. || 490 ||
Śrīcchanda, Vṛttabhadra, Śrīkānta, Śrīpratiṣṭhita, Śrībhadra, Śiracchanda, Gopura, and Sarvadākṛti. (491)
Viṣṇucchanda, Saubhadra, Kailāsa, Candramas, Rudrachanda, and Lalita—these are considered the divine meters (daivikāmatāḥ). || 492 ||
Sumerucchandaka, Śrīkūṭa, Kumbha, Jayāṅga, Vimalāṅga, and Vimalākṛti; || 493 ||
The Haṃsa-chanda, the Chanda, and the Garuḍa-chanda;
the Padmāṅga, the Padmabhadra, the Śarya, and the Kukkuṭakāntaka. || 494 ||
Rudrakānta, Yogabhadra, Bhoṭicchanda, Sudarśana, Skandakānda, Vindhyacakra, Merukūṭa, and Mahendraka. || 495 ||
