The conduct consisting of the observer of the world has the form of the solar orb;
that form which resides perfectly upon the seat in the vessel of space—|| 507 ||
Therefore, the entire great seat (mahāpīṭha) is centered at the southern gate;
it is the support of all the deities, endowed with the pericarp of a lotus.
Having always meditated upon my form—which is established on the feet, pure, having the nature of the Jñānamudrā, and situated in the center of my entire self—[one attains liberation]. || 509 ||
My entire form and appearance is centered within the nature of the *bindu*;
my supreme and most excellent [abode] is the gateway on the right, the seat of the *mālā*.
Residing at the southern gate, he has the nature of the eternal Giver;
he is the form of creation situated within the abodes of all the gods, and is perfectly proportioned.
In the center of the form of the seat (pīṭha) is the Sound (nāda), whose nature is dance;
and in the center of the circle of the heart is the most beautiful form of Sound.

I bow to the Supreme Guru, who assumes the form of a drop from the *tāṇḍava* dance of the Vedas, who is the beautiful mandala, the abode of the assembly, the eternal light, and the one whose nature is perpetual dance.
The excellent food offering, fashioned with wealth, consists of five streams;
it is pure, situated within a preeminent celestial chariot, and located at the southern gate of the temple.
One should worship the Supreme Lord as the *sumantraka* residing within the *sumantra*.
The *liṅga* is said to consist of *nāda*, while the *pīṭha* is of the nature of *bindu*. (515)
Likewise, in the absence of a liṅga or a pedestal, one should contemplate that form within them.
The sequence for the purification of the liṅga has been declared; now hear the sequence for the purification of the mantra.
All mantras beginning with the eyebrows and ending with the salutation (namaskāra) are prescribed;
they should be employed at the time of ritual action, and one should perform their purification.
(From PDF 58, p.
707) And indeed, the excellence [of the mantra] is designated by the name *praṇava*.
It is well-established that the entire mantra is the *praṇava*, which is the primordial name. (518)
Truth, truth: one should always chant my meditation, the Praṇava;
for everything shall be my own form—the pure and imperishable Oṃkāra.
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the letter *m*— along with the *bindu* and *nāda*—
should be known as the supreme *praṇava*, consisting of five deities through their union.
The letter *a* resides in the heart; the letter *u* is designated as being in the throat;
the letter *m* is situated in the middle of the palate; and the *bindu* is established between the eyebrows. || 521 ||
Nāda and Lalāṭaka are indeed the supreme five syllables of Yoga.
The letter A is the face of Sadyojāta, and the letter U is the face of Vāmadeva.
The letter *ma* is the terrible face (*ghoravaktra*), while the *bindu* is the face of Tatpuruṣa;
the *nāda* is the face of Īśāna, and that which transcends the *nāda* is Naṭeśvara.
The subtle five-syllabled mantra has been declared; now hear the gross five-syllabled mantra:
the syllable *na* is the Sadyojāta face, while the syllable *ma* is the Ghoravaktra face.
The letter Śi is the face of Īśa, the letter Va is the left face, and the letter Ya is the face of Puruṣa; thus, it becomes the glorious five-syllabled mantra.
The letter *sa* is Vāmadeva, established as the nature of the three principles (*tritattva*).
Within the group of seed-syllables of space (*ākāśa*), there shall be a twelve-syllable mantra.
The six limbs of Brahman are short, while the eye is long with a bindu;
the weapon-mantra is all-knowing, ending in the visarga and without a bindu.
One should apply the sixth and the thirteenth [syllables] auspiciously to the fifth;
it is joined with the elision of the beginning, the elision of the end, and the elision of the middle. (528)
(From PDF 59, p.
708) This is proclaimed as the mantra of the vowels and consonants along with their case-endings:
the letter *ha* is the form of Śiva, while the letter *sa* is the form of Śakti. (529)

One should join the mantra of Śiva consisting of the letter *ha*, which has the *bindu* and *nāda* as its mouth, together with the letter *sa* joined by the *visarga*, and Śiva who is the recipient. || 530 ||
The fourteenth [vowel] joined with the fire of the east (the letter *ra*) and the *nāda*,
along with the *bindu* and *nāda*, constitutes the syllable of sixteen phonemes.
This mantra of Ambā has been proclaimed; now hear the procedure for the nine-syllable [mantra]:
the letter at the end of 'sa' (ha) joined with the letter at the end of 'ha' (la), followed by the third letter of the sky (kha).
The fifth vowel of the sixth [syllable], ending with the letter *ya*, along with the two [syllables] of Varuṇa and Anala;
the letter *ma* endowed with the sixth vowel, accompanied by the bindu and nāda. (533)
This nine-syllable mantra has been declared; now hear the procedure for the eight-syllable one:
the fourth letter of the eighth [syllable], and the very letter preceding it. (534)
The serpent-like, peak-syllable, lovely one, which is the fifth of the sixth class, joined with the sixth and the fourteenth—this is the auspicious eight-syllable mantra. (535)
Then, O Maheśvara, hear the Śārabha mantra, which is fierce:
it consists of the fifth [consonant] five times, followed by the second letter of the seventh group. (536)
The thirteenth element of the sixteenth [syllable], the middle one, and its group, the sixth;
the peak-long [vowel] beginning with the seventh, and the peak-long ending with *vaṣaṭ*. (537)
Having performed the previously mentioned worship and offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter,
one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) joined with the twelve-syllable mantra.
One should perform rites for nourishment in the eastern quarter, while incantations for causing enmity are performed in the southeast;
those for attraction in the southern region, and likewise, those for bewilderment in the southwest.
(From PDF 60, p.
709) Peaceful rites (*śāntikarma*) are to be performed in the western direction (*vāruṇī*); likewise, the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*) in the northwest (*anila*);
the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*) should be employed in the north (*saumya*); and similarly, the rite of killing (*māraṇa*) in the northeast (*īśāna*). || 540 ||
Know that spring resides in the forenoon, summer likewise in midday,
the rainy season in the afternoon, and the cool season in the twilight.
Midnight corresponds to the autumn season, and dawn to the winter;
perform summoning during spring, and effect inciting enmity during summer.

The rite of eradication (uccāṭana) should be performed during the rainy season, as well as the rite of killing (māraṇa) in the winter; the rite of pacification (śāntika) is for the autumn season, and likewise, the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika) in the early winter.
Having attained the fruit of the sequence of the Dharma, one should contemplate the dance of another;
one should perform the rite of fire-oblation (homa) in the northeast of the southern abode.
In the four directions, with those who recite the praises and auspicious hymns of the four Vedas,
one should constantly offer oblations for six months or even for a single month, performing the rites of the fire-sacrifice.
Having recited the three syllables once, listen now to the sequence of the name-mantra:
*nāda*, *sanāda*, *nādādya*, and the fifth letter of the sixth group [of consonants]. (546)
The first syllable of the fourth [vowel] endowed with the eleventh vowel, and the seed-syllable of the eighth [vowel] joined with its own long root-vowel. (547)
The seed-syllable of the seventh [letter], preceded by the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with *namaḥ*,
is this secret name-mantra established as the supreme light.
This is exceedingly secret and not to be given away; it is the name of the Lord who transcends all mantras.
This mantra, whose essence is Śiva, is to be bestowed upon those who are my devotees. (549)
The sequence of the name-mantras has been declared; now hear the ritual procedure of the Vīra-tantra:
the third letter of the second [varga], endowed with the bindu and the nāda. (550)
(From *pdf* 61, p.
710) This Vīra-tantra has been proclaimed; now listen to the sequence of protective mantras.
The seed-syllable at the end of the fifth [group], and the seed-syllable that is the fifth of the sixth [group]. (551)
The third and fourth [letters] of the eighth [vowel], and the first seed-syllable of the seventh [vowel] joined with my second letter. (552)
The sequence of protective mantras has been declared; now hear the sequence of Brahma-mantras: the third letter of the sixth group, conjoined with the fire of dissolution (the letter *ra*). (553)
Listen to the procedure for the Viṣṇu-mantra, which is joined with Bindu and Nāda:
the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu is Vāgbhava (AIM), adorned with Bindu as its crest-ornament. (554)
One should employ [the mantra] beginning with the *praṇava* (Om), ending with *namaḥ*, and in the dative case;
this is declared to be the Viṣṇu-mantra. Now listen to the sequence for the wealth-mantras. || 555 ||
The fourth [syllable] of the fifth [group], endowed with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, is this mantra of wealth; now hear the sequence of the Lakṣmī-mantra. || 556 ||
The primary seed-syllable of the eighth [letter], conjoined with the fire of dissolution (ra), joined with the fourth vowel (ī), and endowed with the bindu and nāda. || 557 ||
This mantra of Lakṣmī has been declared; now listen to the sequence of the mantra of Skanda.
The seventh letter of the *ya*-group is the seed-syllable, conjoined with the fifth vowel. (558)

The second [syllable] of the seventh [group], however, is joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*; this entire mantra, consisting of the essence of Śiva, begins with one's own name and ends with "namaḥ. (559)
The sequence for the purification of the mantra has been declared; now listen to the characteristics of the seat.
The first syllable of the seed-syllable of space is the mantra, which is the root-cause of the process of emanation.
Then, for him, everything arises from the Divine;
it is born of power (śaktika), established upon the foundational power (ādhāna-śakti), independent, and originating from Dharma and the other [qualities].
(From PDF 62, p.
711) Listen to [the description of] the seat and so forth for the purpose of the signs of meditative worship (dhyānapūjā).
O Goddess, that which is the chapter on the world is like the root, having been released from bondage. (562)
He has four faces and eight arms, with the luster of molten gold;
he possesses twelve syllables, and his hair is bound upward at the crown of his head.

One should visualize the Śakti seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), holding a noose, a goad, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a thunderbolt, a chisel, a javelin, and the gesture of supreme knowledge (jñānamudrā).
The wise preceptor should meditate upon Śakti, who is adorned with all ornaments, who is the sole refuge of all the worlds, and whose form is the foundational support.
The seed-syllable of Śakti, the sprout, the stalk, and the elements beginning with dharma are to be avoided.
Śakti is the color of saffron, and the seed-syllable resembles coral.
The sprout is silver-colored and the stalk resembles lapis lazuli;
it is joined with the feet beginning with Dharma, situated both below and above.
The foundational power (ādhāraśakti) is situated in the hand, described along with the fivefold seat;
first is the seat called Ananta, and after that, the lion-throne (siṃhāsana).
The third is the yogic posture (yogāsana), and after that is the lotus posture (padmāsana);
the fifth is declared to be the pure (vimala) [posture], which one should arrange by proceeding upwards.
The seat called Ananta is circular and situated one above the other;
joined with eight nāgas, it is called the Anantāsana. || 570 ||
The seat named Ananta has been proclaimed; now hear the sequence of the Lion Throne (siṃhāsana).
It consists of the fourfold [powers]: dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya. || 571 ||
Dharma is the true nature of reality, while knowledge is indeed the form of the elephant;
detachment shall be the form of the lion, and sovereignty the form of the horse. || 572 ||
Each [lion] was surrounded by millions upon millions of lions, and all of them were of the very nature of rājāvarta [sapphire]. (573)
The fourfold group consisting of the Unmanifest (avyakta), Niyati, Kāla,
and Kalā should be placed in order upon the four corners of the square in the cardinal directions.
Keśava [described] the auspicious lion-throne (siṃhāsana) of the middle foot in this manner;
the sequence of the lion-throne has been declared—now hear the procedure for the yoga-seat (yogāsana). || 575 ||
That seat is pure, shaped like a tortoise, and the color of fire;
one should first place the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) there, and likewise the syllable *a* in the fire.
The letter Ā is in the southern quarter, and likewise the letter I in the south-west;
the letter Ī is in the western quarter, and the letter U in the region of the wind (north-west).
One should place the letter *ū* in the northern direction, the letters *ṛ* and *lṛ* in the northeastern region, and the letter *ṛ* in the center; thus there shall be the yogic seat (*yogāsana*).
Thus the yogic posture has been described; now hear the procedure for the lotus posture (padmāsana).
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and Kalavikaraṇī— || 579 ||
Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathanī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, and the ninth, Manonmanī. || 580 ||
One should place [the letters] upon the tips of the filaments and in the pericarp in due order.
Thus the lotus posture (padmāsana) has been described; now hear about the stainless posture (vimalāsana).
One should worship Gaṇāmbikā in the north and Mahādevī in the east; "Tanno Gaurī" in the south and "Pracodayāt" in the west.
One should conceive of the pure seat as pervaded by these powers:
the position of the sun is in the midst of fire, and the moon is in the midst of the sun. (583)
(From PDF 64, p.
713) Darkness is in the middle of passion, and within that, goodness alone;
[he perceives] the self, the inner self, and the supreme self. (584)
The three principles of the Self have been declared; now hear the sequence of the principles of knowledge (vidyā-tattva).
One should install Brahmavidyā, Śivavidyā, and Guruvidyā in their proper order.
The principle of Brahmā is below that, the principle of Viṣṇu is above it;
beyond that is the principle of Rudra, and above that is Maheśvara. (586)
The principle called Sādākhya is at its summit; beyond that is the principle of Bindu. Above that is the principle of Nāda, and beyond that is the principle of Śakti.
One should worship that supreme Śivatattva, which bestows knowledge and liberation;
in its center is the abode of the Eye, and in its center is the seat of flowers.
Then there is the seat, exceedingly pure with its many parts, possessing the luster of crystal;
it is circular, the form of Sadāśiva, having the nature of space, and higher than the highest.
Listen to the sequence of Śiva’s creation in the form of the *bindu* alone:
the *nāda* resides within the *bindu*, and the *dhvani* resides within the *nāda*. (590)
And the Self, situated within the resonance (dhvani), is beyond infinity, higher than the highest, Śiva, the supreme and subordinate Brahman, immeasurable and blameless. || 591 ||
Incomparable, subtle, eternal, omnipresent, and sovereign;
because of its purity, it is called Śiva—the highest of the high, beyond the supreme. (592)
Because of its nature as Brahman and because of its being the Supreme Spirit, it is designated as "Brahman";
because it is distinct from all means of valid cognition, Naṭeśvara is the unmeasurable.
Because it is impure, it should be known as censurable; because it is impure, it is exceedingly censurable.
It is incomparable and peerless, having resorted to the southern direction.
(Beyond the Void, p. 714) It is subtler than that which transcends the void, eternal because it is devoid of a cause;
it is said to be all-pervading due to its omnipresence, and it is called the Lord (prabhu) because of its sovereignty. || 595 ||
For the sake of protecting the world until the end of the creation, as the cause of the world's origin, and for the benefit of practitioners, he assumed a body by his own will. (596)
For the sake of protection, he obtained from Ambā the wonderful Dakṣiṇeśvara, the Lord who dwells in the assembly hall,
who is eternally active, and who is a great light.
Śiva, the supreme cause, who abides in the midst of the form of bliss, is then declared to be threefold; and furthermore, he is likewise partless (niṣkala).
Both the *sakala* (with parts) and the *niṣkala* (without parts), as well as the *sakala* in its proper sequence;
the *niṣkala* has four divisions, and the *sakala* likewise in its proper sequence. (599)
The Sakala, Niṣkala, and Tvaika are proclaimed in sequence as the ninefold [forms].
From the thousandth part of the Śiva-tattva, that which is named Śānti arises.
They say that power (śakti) is the maker of power; these are its synonymous designations.
And from that very thousandth part, the name "Power" (Śakti) has arisen.
Furthermore, Śakti and Vidyā are declared to be synonyms for that;
and from a thousandth part of that very [Vidyā], the manifestation of the form of Nāda arises.
Sound (nāda) and its foundation (pratiṣṭhā) are proclaimed as synonyms;
and from that very thousandth part, the principle of the drop (bindu-tattva) arises.
*Bindu* and *nivṛtti* are synonyms that express it;
having taken hold of the supreme state, [the Lord] always performs the *tāṇḍava* dance with excellent qualities. (604)
Their essential natures are unmanifest, and likewise they are devoid of activity due to that characteristic;
thus, the fourth is indeed called the Śivatattva, which is partless (niṣkala). || 605 ||
(From PDF 66, p.
715) "O Maheśvara, meditation-worship is without support and partless.
Thus the partless has been described; it is remembered as the supreme state. (606)
Therefore, from a single portion of that [portion], the emergence of the Sādākhya occurs;
the Vīra-liṅga is, in its mode, characterized by the principle of Sādākhya.
In the *liṅga*, Sadāśiva has arisen as the essence of *nāda*;
and in the *pīṭha*, Śakti has arisen by the name Manonmanī.
In both the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*), Śiva and Śakti arise;
thus, the *liṅga* is indeed masculinity, while the pedestal is the very principle of femininity.
The Liṅga and the Pīṭha are partless (niṣkala), while Śakti and Śambhu are with parts (sakala);
the partless is devoid of parts, whereas the one with parts is endowed with parts.

For the sake of meditation, worship, and ritual purpose, it is traditionally taught that [the deity] possesses both parts (sakala) and is partless (niṣkala) for ascetics, mantra-practitioners, the wise, and yogis.
One should always worship the Lord of Gods according to the method of the Liṅga-pīṭha;
[namely] the path of letters (varṇādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), the path of principles (tattvādhvan), and the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan). || 612 ||
The path of mantra and the path of kalā constitute the essential nature of Sādākhya;
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe the sequence of the stages on these paths and their specific characteristics.
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) consists of the verses on the principles (tattvagāthās); that which was mentioned above as "the feet" is likewise the head.
The path of principles (tattvādhvan) is the heart, while the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is the hair of the body. 614.
The path of mantra is the support of blood; the path of kalā consists of semen, marrow, and bone;
and the path of kalā likewise constitutes all the limbs—thus is the form of Sādākhya.
Endowed with thirty-eight digits (kalās), it exists as the manifest whole (sakala);
then one should conceive of Sadāśiva, beginning from Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta.
One should fashion the five heads with the Īśāna mantra, and one should fashion the four faces with the Puruṣa mantra. (617)
One should assign the heart centers with the Aghora mantra;
one should assign the secret and other limbs with the Vāmadeva mantra.
One should assign the limbs, beginning with the feet, using the Sadyojāta and other mantras:
[the divisions are] eighteen, thirteen, eight, four, and five.
The unborn [powers] known as Vāmā and Ghorā are remembered as the digits (kalās) of the Lord of Men (Puruṣeśa).
Thus, the manifest (sakala) has been declared; now follows the auspicious unmanifest (niṣkala) Tāṇḍava.
Through the conceptualization of hands, feet, belly, and so forth, the wise know him as the complete one;
he is Sādākya, the Lord of all gods, manifest and facing in every direction.
He resides in the center of the pericarp of a thousand-petaled lotus;
he is youthful, five-headed, ten-armed, and four-faced.
Having twelve eyes, four arms, and endowed with four faces,
two feet, the appearance of crystal, and a white sacred thread.
Resembling ten million suns and endowed with the digit of the moon of gnosis,
he holds in his right hands the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, an axe, a vajra, and a sword.
Holding a shield, a goad, and a noose in [his left hands], and a staff and the gesture of granting boons in the others; he is cool with moonbeams, gentle, and clothed in white garments. (625)
Wearing a turban and an upper garment, adorned with all ornaments,
complete in every limb, and anointed with all fragrant unguents.
He is the inner self of all beings, eternally contemplated as the non-dual reality;
he is the presiding deity of the five elements and has the nature of the five Brahmas.
(From PDF 68, p.
717) Endowed with these characteristics—such as the five syllables and so forth, the instruction, the Beloved of Pārvatī, and the Supreme—Sādākhya is indeed the essential nature itself. 628.
On his very left side is the primordial power Manonmanī;
just as fire possesses the quality of heat, this power also belongs to the All-pervading Lord.
There is no Śiva devoid of power, nor [is there] anything devoid of Śiva.

The constituent parts of the cosmic egg, the sciences (*vidyās*), the lords of knowledge (*vidyeśas*), the lords of the hosts (*gaṇeśas*), and the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) together with their weapons—all these have arisen from him in succession. (631)
All of them were clothed in their respective qualities and endowed with their respective insignia;
they were complete in all their limbs, possessing a radiance like that of infinite suns.
Thus, the form of Sadāśiva, together with the Liṅga and the Pīṭha, has been described; however, the power of that which is called Sādākhya cannot be fully described.
The Sakala (with parts) and Niṣkala (without parts) have been declared; now hear about the Sakala.
The forms beginning with Īśvara are celebrated as the Sakala.
Whatever has been declared regarding Sadāśiva is likewise said concerning Īśvara; one should arrange the enclosure beginning with Brahmā exactly as before. || 635 ||
One should fashion images from wood, metal, or stone;
[one should contemplate] Śambhu, who abides in the reality of the Vidyā, endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
One should know that the *liṅga* is the *golaka*, and Maheśvara is indeed the *sakala*;
at the conclusion of the *liṅga*-worship, one should worship Īśvara in due order.
It is said that Rudra’s manifestation arises from a thousandth part of Īśvara;
he has four arms and three eyes, and his crest is adorned with the crescent moon. (638)
The gods, radiant as lightning, hold axes and deer-skins as weapons;
they are complete in all their limbs and adorned with every ornament. (639)
On the northern side of Umādenī, endowed with all auspicious marks,
the essence of Brahman arises from a ten-millionth part of Īśvara.
He has four arms and four faces, wears a crown of matted hair, holds a water-pot and a rosary, is blood-red in color, and possesses beautiful eyes. (641)
Sāvitrī, Bhāratī, and Pārśvasṛṣṭimūrti are remembered as such;
Rudra is the embodiment of withdrawal (saṃhāra), and Viṣṇu is the embodiment of maintenance (sthiti). || 642 ||
The one renowned as Sṛṣṭimūrti and Brahmā are considered to be the threefold forms;
these three forms are said to be established within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 643 ||

The partless (niṣkala) is the place of dissolution; the "A" sound is both with-part (sakala) and partless. The place of enjoyment (bhoga), however, is with-part, characterized by the authority over dissolution and enjoyment.
The wondrous Dakṣiṇeśvara is said to be "beyond parts" (paraniṣkala);
indeed, you are recited as both "with parts" (sakala) and "without parts" (niṣkala), as well as the "other" (apara).
The Destroyer of the Noose (Pāśahā), who is capable of constantly approaching the dance of others, [is followed] by three deities, from whom the thirty-three [gods] subsequently arise. (646)
First, the eleven Rudras, joined by the twelve Ādityas,
the eight Vasus, and the two Aśvins— these are the thirty-three deities.
And thirty thousand crores of deities are there among the three forms;
indeed, they create the bodies of the gods from the essence of the elements.

O Lord of Gods, the cause of all, having meditated upon the Lord as the dancing Tāṇḍava, one's sovereignty—which might otherwise be destroyed by the connection with impurity—shall instead bring awakening to the heart. (649)
Then one should invoke the God, who holds flowers in his hand and is seated on a comfortable throne;
having recollected the root mantra and meditated upon the Supreme, [one realizes] Sadāśiva, the all-pervading. (650)
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva as supreme, one should cause him to descend by means of the Sadyojāta mantra;
one should perform the installation with the Vāmadeva mantra and restrain him with the Aghora mantra.
The presence [of the deity] is through the person, but the worship is performed by Īśāna;
just as the fire situated within the hearth is made to blaze up by the wind. (652)
In that very same way, the Lord Śiva is born through the name-mantra;
he is invoked by the invocation [mudrā], and established by the establishing mudrā.
Then follow the five-faced cow-mudrā, the śakti-mudrā,
the niṣṭhunā-liṅga-mudrā, the lotus-eye-mudrā, and the weapon-mudrā.
One should perform the Nyāsa as before with the five Brahmans and the six limbs, and one should likewise offer perfume, flowers, incense, and a lamp. || 655 ||
O Maheśvara, listen now to this specific distinction regarding the door of the *liṅga*:
the base of the *liṅga* is said to be the feet, and the tip of the *liṅga* is called the mouth. (656)
The two sides of the thread are the four arms, and the end of the thread is said to be the back.
To the right of Īśvara, however, is Brahmā, intent upon the work of creation. (657)
From the left side of Īśvara, Viṣṇu arises as the cause of maintenance;
from the nose, Vāyu is produced, and from the two ears, the ten directions.
He who was born from the lotus-hand is celebrated as Gaṇeśa;
Bhāskara was born from their heart, and [the third] was produced from the navel. || 659 ||
Indra, however, was produced from the back; Agni was born from the right eye; and the god known as Soma was born from the left eye. (660)
The Yakṣas and gods are in the two breasts; the Rudras are in the right eye;
the emergence of weapons is from the tips of the hands; and those born from the nails are from Rati. (661) (PDF 71, p. 720)
From the thighs were born the sages, those who originated from the *jānu* (knees); from the feet arose all the gods and the emergence of the knowledge of Śiva. (662)
At the time of withdrawal, one should worship the primordial Tāṇḍava-liṅga, which is everything;
one should worship the Sādākhya within the midst of the nature of the Liṅga-form.
O Maheśvara, I shall describe the sequence of meditation upon Mahāsadāśiva:
he who has five faces and five heads, with three eyes in each face. (664)
He is serene, possessing sixteen arms and a single body, four cubits in height, with eight ears and two feet, and a face slightly smiling. (665)

The trident, the thunderbolt, the sword, and the battle-axe, as well as the wheel and the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), [he holds] in his right hands in sequence for the sake of dispelling fear. 666.
And with his left hands, he bears the fierce serpent, a noose, a bow, a goad, two shields, the gesture of granting boons, and an expression of wonder.
Endowed with the primordial power (Ādi-śakti) and having a black serpent as his sacred thread,
one should install him auspiciously as before with the Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and other mantras.
Having recited the *sadyojāta* mantra, one should offer water for the feet at the [deity's] feet;
with the *vakra* mantra, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth in the [deity's] mouths.
One should offer the arghya on the heads with the Īśāna mantra;
the fragrance on the faces with the Vāma mantra, and the flower on the heads with the Īśāna mantra.
O Maheśvara, one should offer incense with the Sadyojāta mantra, a lamp with the Ghorānu-nāda, and the food offering (naivedya) with the Vaktṛ-mantra, in this sequence.
(From PDF 72, p.
721) One should prepare milk mixed with cardamom, camphor, jasmine, and sandalwood, accompanied by the five Brahmans and the six limbs, using the *dhenu-mudrā*. 672.
Uttering the seed-syllable of the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), which is the phoneme-mantra,
and having uttered the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, one should worship it in the water-vessel.
Subsequently, with the mantras of Īśa and the others, one should gradually perform the consecration;
one should cause the water for sipping (ācamana) and the offering of honor (arghya) to be presented at the four corners in the four directions.
Cow urine has Brahmā as its presiding deity; cow dung has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity;
milk has Rudra as its presiding deity; and curd is said to have Maheśa as its presiding deity.
One should present fragrant flowers and other offerings intended for the deity known as Sarpissāda;
furthermore, one should display the food offering (naivedya) consisting of the five essences and the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā).
One should recite the *Sadasaspatyam*, the *Śaṃ ca le*, the *Āvo rājānam*, and the *Tryambakam* hymns.
The procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) has been declared; now hear the rule for the water with fruit (*phalodaka*).
The bilva and the kadalī, two nāraṅgas, the fruit of the mango and the kelī, and the water from the fruit of the tintriṇī; || 678 ||
Having recited the name-mantra, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
The ritual for fruit-water has been declared; now hear the ritual for seed-water.
Barley, millet, mung beans, rice, white mustard, and *aṅgula*—
this water containing fragrant *hemaśālī* seeds is auspicious.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the root-mantra, the procedure for the "seed-water" (bījodaka) has been declared; now hear the procedure for the "jewel-water" (ratnodaka).
Māṇikya, gomeda, puṣparāga, gāruḍa, coral, crystal, sapphire, pearl, and the auspicious water of jewels; 682.
(From PDF 73, p.

722) One should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth, using the *varṇamantra*. Thus has the water of jewels (*ratnodaka*) been described; now hear the procedure for the scented water (*gandhodaka*). || 683 ||
Sandalwood, kuṣṭha, and likewise takkola and saffron; camphor, picchilā, musk, and likewise agallochum. || 684 ||
One should offer uśīra, cloves, and likewise campaka buds, as well as perfumes and other items for the food offering (naivedya), using the name-mantra. || 685 ||
Thus has the ritual of scented water been described; now hear the procedure for the water of flowers:
the *caṃpaka*, the *prasava*, the *mallikā*, and the *pāṭalī*. (686)
The ketakī, the mountain flower (giripuṣpa), the punnāga, and the kunda;
the nandyāvarta, the śriyāvarta, the mandāra, and the karavīraka. || 687 ||
One should offer jasmine, blue lotus, and lotus, mixed with hiri, berya, and other ingredients, along with perfume, flowers, and incense, using the Śiva-mantra. (688)
Thus has the offering of flowers and water been described; now hear the procedure for the worship with food. Now follows the consecration with foods, which increases longevity and health. (689)
Food is the essence of life, supreme, and the foundation for all living beings;
therefore, this auspicious consecration with food is what brings me joy. (690)
The specific form of food is indeed my own form, remembered as being twofold;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a more excellent rite for the worship of food.
Therefore, with every effort, one should consecrate [the deity] with food alone; having offered food in the form and shape of a linga, along with perfumes, flowers, and incense.
One should offer a lamp, milk-rice, and betel leaf;
this daily rite of food-offering is auspicious and the cause of all success. (693)
(From PDF 74, p.
723) The *apamṛtyujaya* [rite] brings joy and bestows prosperity upon the king and the kingdom;
it is a great source of food and flowers, and is the supreme means for propitiating the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (694)
The Guru [teaches] that food-worship (annārcana) is pure, brings all peace, and is victorious; because it is the supreme seed-syllable of the Mother (Ambā), it is therefore called "food" (anna). 695.
He who performs the worship with food attains the supreme goal;
therefore, one should worship with food itself with every effort. (696)
Having performed the washing of the food, one should sequentially place the root-mantra (mūlabīja);
then one should offer perfume, flowers, incense, and a lamp.
Having touched [the disciple] with the five Brahmans, one should bind the cow-seal (dhenu-mudrā) upon him;
while reciting the name-mantra, one should sprinkle [him] very gradually.
Having worshipped the one whose gender and form are indistinct, and having meditated upon Dakṣiṇeśvara before him while pronouncing his name,
one should offer incense and flowers.
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) ending with incense and lamps while pronouncing the name;
one should recite the two mantras beginning with "pūṣā" for everything in every case. (700)
The ritual procedure for the offering of food has been declared; now hear the ritual procedure for the worship with water.
Water consecrated as before is filled in a golden vessel. (701)
Alternatively, one should install Dakṣiṇeśvara in the center of water contained within a vessel made of silver, copper, or a sacrificial wood.
O Maheśvara, having caused the dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, and flowers to be consecrated with mantras one hundred thousand times,
one should cause perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps to be offered.
The water-offering is a great secret, providing stability and being most auspicious;
it is pure, bestows all accomplishments, and destroys all diseases. || 704 ||
*Triyambakaṃ*, *Imā rudraṃ*, *Āpo hi ṣṭhā*, *Śaṃ no devīḥ*, *Iḷe dyāvāpṛthivī*, *Kad rudrāya*, *Namaḥ sahasrākṣāya*, and *Sadasas patiḥ*. (705)
Jātavedas, Īśāna, Haṃsa, Ātadeva, Śepa, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Vāma, Sadyojāta, and Svādiṣṭhā thereafter. (706)
"Sahasraśīrṣā," "Annapaté," "Pūṣan," "Imā agniḥ," "Ile," "Ye devāḥ," "Anno amānaḥ," "Gaurīrmimāya," and "Deva āśāḥ"—these [are the verses]. || 707 ||
O Agni, you [should recite] "ā vo rājānam" and likewise "mṛtaṃ tat savituḥ";
one should chant this Bṛhat Sāman beginning with the syllable Om as "oṃ". (708)
Having recited each of the thirty-six mantras individually once for the purpose of consecration in their proper order, one should sprinkle [the disciple] very slowly.
The ritual procedure for water-worship has been declared; now the characteristics of the vessels are being described:
they may be made of gold, silver, or likewise originating from copper.
A conch shell, or even mother-of-pearl, or likewise the horn of a cow,
or even one made of clay— a bathing vessel such as these is praised.
The middle [vessel] is filled completely with the recited mantra and filled with Śiva;
the lowest is filled with an *āḍhaka* [measure]; indeed, all [of this] shall become one *āḍhaka*.
One should fill conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and horn-horns with their own respective measures;
one should wrap everything with thread so that the intervals between them resemble lattice windows.
Having prepared the sacrificial mound according to the rules with unbroken rice grains and sesame seeds,
one should arrange separate water-pots, either one *āḍhaka* or half of that amount for each.
One should take half a measure of śāli rice, and likewise half of that in sesame;
these, together with sacrificial grass (kūrca), cloth, and jewels, should be placed upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
The preceptor should worship the jars, which have been especially adorned.
At the mouth of the jar is the deity Rudra; in the middle is the deity Mādhava. (716) (Pdf 76, p. 725)
The Pṛṣṭha-laud should belong to Prajāpati, and the presiding deities of the water-jar (kalaśa) are [to be worshipped];
one should cause perfume, flowers, and incense to be offered with the Hṛdaya-mantra. || 717 ||
And [one should worship] Mahādarpa in wine, or Naṭeśvara at the tip of the linga;
[one should worship] Īśvara, who, though formless, abides in form, at the southern gate. || 718 ||
One should perform the consecration with excellent unguents either upon a mirror or a fine image;
these two secret places of worship are the wonderful southern abode.
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe the sequence of consecration and its specific details:
having uttered the name-mantra while recollecting the three-syllable mantra. (720)
Having bathed [the deity] with pure water from the tips of one's hands, measured by the tip of a cow's horn, one should worship [it] and likewise apply fragrant unguents.
One should cause fragrant, pure incense to be offered,
and then one should slowly, very slowly, perform the consecration with pure scented waters.
Having recited the name-mantra once, one should place a flower upon [the deity's] head;
at that time, one should also cause the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya) to be presented.
Having taken a clean cloth, one should fashion the garment-seal;
one should then insert that garment into the linga-base, the ground, and the site itself.
Having taken up the weapon-mantra of entry, one should cause it to be offered to Caṇḍeśa;
with the mantra "vāstoṣpate," one should worship Vāstunātha.
With the mantras "etonvindrastu vāmā," "āpo hiṣṭhā," and so forth, one should perform the sprinkling;
then, having taken a fine cloth, one should bind it with the heart-mantra.

Having wrapped the *liṅga* with a cloth, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* in sequence, starting from the portion representing one-fourth of the cloth and beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta. (727)
From Manonmanī up to the end of the sacred seats (pīṭhas), one should apply the Tripuṇḍra of the limbs (aṅgas) and so forth;
at the conclusion of that, one should offer a mirror while reciting the Śakti mantra.
Having uttered the Aghora mantra, one should cause the sacrifice to be offered;
thereafter, one should cause the parasol and the fly-whisk to be presented with the Hṛdaya mantra. || 729 ||
Having recited the Vāyu mantra, one should cause the two sandals to be offered;
thereafter, one should present a handful of flowers with the mudrā known as the salutation.
Then, having performed an embrace, one should cause the *jñānamudrā* to be bestowed;
one should offer vessels of flames with the head and with both hands. (731)
The supreme Rudra-prostitute and the celibate student should maintain [the ritual];
one should place a lamp in the eastern direction within water contained in a golden pitcher. || 732 ||
One should present [the offering] joined with all musical instruments upon the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
Then, having made a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), the characteristics of recitation (japa) are described. || 733 ||
Japa is declared to be of two kinds for all those who desire to perform japa: that which is mental, and that which is vocal—either whispered or clearly articulated. (734)
One should prepare an offering (naivedya) directed toward the ninefold path;
having worshipped in the morning and at dawn, one should likewise present the offering at midday.
Having cooked two *prasthas* at that time, one should offer them;
there should be one lamp at the two daily times, and two lamps at night. (736)
At dawn and at midday, he should offer two *prasthas* of rice as an oblation;
and having worshipped her in the evening, the lamp should be made twofold.
One should offer two *prasthas* at each of the two times; the lamps are said to be four, but at evening they should be doubled. (738)
For the medium [grade of worship] at the lowest [level], it is prescribed that the sacrificial offering (havis) at midday shall be one āḍhaka;
at two times of day, it shall be two prasthas, and the lamp shall consist of twenty [pala].

In the three middle [circles], however, the wise and intelligent one should perform the offering of oblations (balidāna) three times a day, accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and using the emblem of the oblation (baliliṅga).
One should know that the medium-of-the-medium [offering] consists of the oblation (havis) offered at the three times;
the twenty-four lamps consist of half a watch (ardhayāma) and half of that. || 741 ||
The worship performed at midnight is said here to last for one and a half watches;
it consists of offerings of flowers, food, and unbroken rice (akṣata) accompanied by oblations (bali) during the three periods of the day in due order.
Accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and endowed with dance and song,
at midday there should be a daily fire-oblation provided with incense and lamps.
I shall describe the best [offering] from the medium one: two āḍhakas for each of the three times;
and for the offering at the three times, five parts together with a lamp.

At two times [per day], accompanied by musical instruments and attended by twenty courtesans, one should bring a *droṇa* of grain from the highest to the lowest [class] there; at three times [per day], one should bring a *droṇa*. (745)
During the half-yāma [period] following the *droṇa*, one should offer one hundred and eight lamps;
there should be an offering of food three times a day, accompanied by fire oblations (*homa*) three times a day.
Equipped with all musical instruments and accompanied by dance and song,
there should be one thousand and eight, or one hundred, Rudrakanya maidens.
Endowed with beauty and youth, and adorned with all ornaments,
the women of middle stature [offered] the four oblations there at the three times of day.
(From PDF 79, p.
728) Having cooked milk-rice and other dishes combined with one *droṇa* of rice, and having cooked pure food separately by the measure of one *droṇa*, [one should offer it]. || 749 ||
One should also offer half a *droṇa* of lamps, numbering two hundred;
there should be offerings and oblations (*bali-homa*) at the three times of day, and one should prescribe incense for the enemy of cold (*śītārī*).
It was accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments, proclaiming every auspicious blessing;
it was attended by eight hundred courtesans and filled with the resonant sound of hymns of praise.
Two types of time have been declared; one should perform the dance during the three junctions [of the day].
With reference to the most excellent of the excellent, the sequence for the sacrificial food (haviṣya) is now stated.
Having cooked six droṇas of milk-rice with rice grains alone, and at midnight, five hundred auspicious lamps [should be lit], half of which [are for the first half] and half for the second. (753)
At the two gates and at the three times of day, one should offer pure food and rice;
at the three times, there should be offerings and fire-sacrifices accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
One should especially perform two hundred and sixteen dances;
thus the ninefold [classification] has been declared. Now hear in order about the milk-rice offerings and the rest. (755)
Milk-rice, rice-and-pulse porridge, milk-curd balls, and pure boiled rice—these are the fourfold offerings;
with twice as much milk as rice, it should be combined with plantain fruit.
This is declared to be *pāyasānna* (milk-rice) when it contains one-fourth part of soaked mung beans mixed with jaggery according to one's ability; now hear about *kṛsarānna*.
Having added a fourth part of sesame powder to the rice,
one should cook it according to the prescribed ritual with clarified butter (ājya) equal to a fourth part of that [mixture].
This is declared to be *kṛsarānna*; now hear about *gulānna*:
having prepared half a *bhāra* of jaggery (*gula*) and half a *bhāra* of rice.
One should add half a *gulā* of split mung beans and one *prastha* of milk;
as for the clarified butter, half a *droṇa* or a full *droṇa*—now hear the characteristics of the cook. (80.760)
Having first performed the ritual bath, those devoted to the vow of celibacy,
wearing white sacred threads and white garments, were auspicious.
Having washed his feet with water and six grains of rice,
the wise practitioner should purify [the site] with the principal seed-mantra.
One should fill it with pure water increased by half a portion of rice;
then, one should kindle the fire with the *śikhā* mantra and heat these [vessels] with the *astra* mantra. || 763 ||
Then, with the *puruṣa* mantra, one should [offer] the crown (*maulī*) in the west;
then, with the eye-mantra, one should gaze [at it], and thereafter [consume] the cooked sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Thereafter, one should worship with ghee while recollecting the Vāma mantra;
then, one should examine whether it is well-cooked by means of the Tatpuruṣa mantra. || 765 ||
One should purify the air within the walls of the vessels with the Aghora mantra alone;
one should apply a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) of one finger-breadth to the vessels using ashes.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps;
likewise, one should thoroughly honor the vessels and all the fuel. || 767 ||
With the mantra *huṃ*, the practitioner should raise everything up in sequence and install it in due order on the western side of the pavilion.
One should cause [the offering] to be made with these, as well as with apūpa cakes and other such items,
using either gold, silver, copper, or even a leaf of the plantain tree.
One should fetch either a vessel of pure bell-metal or one made of palāśa wood;
having fashioned three thick legs, with the tripod standing upon its middle part. (770)
(From PDF 81, p.
730) Taking a golden vessel endowed with all auspicious marks, one should fill the great *mahābhadra*—six units in height—with pure cotton. (771)
Having first sprinkled it with clarified butter, one should fill the vessel with food;
the mountain of oblation and the casket should constitute the food offering for Śiva.
Having the appearance of the full moon, split like a mung bean, and containing molasses,
it is accompanied by fruits and all kinds of side dishes, combined with cow's clarified butter.
One should perform the rites of inspection and so forth, and the veiling with the heart-mantra;
then, while reciting the syllable of the heart, one should bind the Saurabhī mudrā. (774)
Having recited the Śiva-mantra once, one should offer it with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra);
the offering for the retinue (parivāra) shall consist of one-fourth of that portion.
The wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with one-fourth of a quarter-part;
here, the remainder in the vessel is said to be one-sixteenth part.
One should offer half [of the remainder] to Śakti, and half of that remaining portion in the vessel;
then, having again given water for sipping (ācamana) with fragrant water.
Thereafter, one should cause betel-leaf to be offered together with all ornaments;
one should cause the leaf to be given with oil and three times as many fruits.
One should cause the offering of fruits and flowers to be presented with devotion;
indeed, one should offer every kind of excellent substance to Caṇḍeśvara.
The remains of Sadāśiva’s offerings (nirmālya) must not be eaten by any living beings;
they may be consumed by animals and elephants, or else they should be cast into the waters.
The attendant should receive the offering intended for all;
just as the remains of one's own teacher are to be eaten, so too are they for the son and the disciple. (781)
Vāmī, Nīlinī, Cakrī, Śaṅkhī, Khaḍgī, and likewise Tvasī—these eleven are declared to be the powers (śaktis) of the inner enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa). (793) [Source: PDF 82, p. 732]
Listen now to the sequence of the deities and the Śakti in the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa):
one should install them in order, beginning from the eastern petal, starting with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin.
Ananta, Sūkṣma, Saṃjña, Ekanetra as spoken by Śiva, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin. (795)
These eight lords of the Vidyās indeed have three eyes and four arms; they carry the ṭaṅka, the trident, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting gesture.
O Lord of Knowledge, the colors for the application [of the tilaka] are, in order: red, white, blue, yellow, black, saffron, crimson, and resembling collyrium. (797)
Bhūśrī, Medhā, Kānti, Prabhā, Tuṣṭi,
as well as Śruti and Medhā— these are the eight powers (śaktis) of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas).
The enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge has been described; now hear of the enclosure of Gaṇeśas.
One should worship Gaurī in the north, and one should worship Vṛṣabha in the east.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa in the south, one should worship Nandīśa in the west;
Mahākāla in the southwest, and Bhṛṅgīśa in the northwest.
One should worship Caṇḍeśa in the northeastern direction and Ṣaṇmukha in the southeastern direction;
she is two-eyed, two-armed, dark-complexioned, and holds a blue lotus in her hand like Gaurī.
He has the color of the lordly bull, possesses sharp horns, and is of great strength;
he has the face of an elephant, three eyes, the luster of saffron, and four arms.
Holding a noose and teeth, you are skilled in *kuśalaḍḍuka*;
four-armed and three-eyed, you resemble the *japā* flower. (803)
(From *pdf* 83, p.
733) Among all the presiding deities of the gates, the illustrious Lord Nandīdeva is the leader;
with palms joined in reverence, the glorious one [holds] the vajra in his hand. || 804 ||
Four-armed and three-eyed, with a luster like that of a dark cloud,
he carries a sword, a thunderbolt, the gesture of fearlessness, and a lance.
Two-armed and two-eyed, endowed with the banner and the gesture of fearlessness, smoke-colored Bhṛṅgin destroys bad dreams. (806)
Caṇḍeśa, the fierce leader, has four arms and three eyes;
he is blue in color, bestows fearlessness, and wields a trident and an axe.
Mahāsena is red in color, possesses six faces, has the peacock as his vehicle,
is endowed with twelve eyes, and bears [weapons] with his twelve arms.
First, [he holds] a trident, a thunderbolt, a sword, an arrow, the gesture of fearlessness, and an axe;
then a bell, a peacock, a shield, a bell, a serpent, and likewise a goad.
Having worshipped the commander of the divine army (Devasenāpati), one should offer rice mixed with molasses (gulānna).
Bhadrā, Vedadhānā, Kuntikāpī, and Mantikā—[these are the deities]. || 810 ||
Mālinī, Virūpī, Mandī, and Caṇḍā are the eight Śaktis; this is declared to be the Gaṇeśa-enclosure. Now hear about the enclosure of the worlds (loka). || 811 ||
One should worship Indra, whose weapon is the thunderbolt, in the east; Agni, together with his spear, in the southeast;
and one should worship Yama, the wielder of the staff, in the south, and Nirṛti, holding a sword, in the southwest.
One should worship Varuṇa, the lord of waters, holding a noose in his hand, in the western quarter;
and Vāyu, holding a goad in his hand, in the northwestern direction.
One should worship Soma with mace in hand in the north-eastern region,
and one should worship Īśāna with trident in hand in the northeastern quarter.
Dark green, red, black, blue, yellow, smoky-grey, white, and smoke-colored are, in order, the radiances of the World Protectors. (815) (PDF 84, p. 734)
The elephant, goat, buffalo, lion, crocodile, deer, horse, and bull are, in order, the eight vehicles of the guardians of the directions. (816)
Śacī, Svāhā, and that goddess [Sarasvatī] were likewise captivated by you;
as were Kālakaṇṭhī, Nīlī, and the goddess Jitakāni. || 817 ||
These powers, in sequence, are proclaimed as the [consorts] of the World-Lords;
thus the enclosure of the World-Lords has been described, and now the enclosure of the Sun is being told.
The Sun-god, the Great Teacher, Brahma, Vighneśvara, Sarasvatī, Jyeṣṭhā, Viṣṇu, and Kṣetrapālaka. || 819 ||
Red is the color of coral, while that which exceeds the color of gold is [yellow];
crystal is smoky-colored, and dark blue has a black luster, in sequence. (820)
Uṣā and Pratyuṣā, Siṃhikī and Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī and Kalyāṇī, Jñānī and Anādadāyinī. || 821 ||
Puṃśrī, Śriyābhrami, Devī, and Supālinī constitute what is called the solar enclosure; now hear from me about the enclosure of weapons.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, as well as the goad,
the mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus— these are the ten weapons.
Śakti and Gadā are female in form; Pāśa and Padma are neuter;
and the remaining [weapons] are male in form, each having one face and two arms. || 824 ||
Yellow, the form of lightning-discharging [Vidyutjihvā], resembling coral and gold, as well as ruby, coral, black, white, and red. || 825 ||
Kālinī and Virūpī, Vāruṇī and Vimukhī likewise, Nīlinī and Sumukhī, as well as Marddanī and Bhṛṅgamālinī. (826) (PDF 85, p. 735)
One should worship this power of the weapons with their respective names and so forth;
this is called the "Weapon-Avatarana" (weapon-enclosure), which one should worship beneath the petals. || 827 ||
One should worship the Seven Mothers between Gaṇa and Lokeśa:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī; || 828 ||
One should worship Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍī, and the seven Mothers, as well as Vīrabhadra and Vighneśa, in the eastern direction. || 829 ||
One should worship the Lord of Yakṣas according to the rules in the northern direction,
and one should cast an offering upon the sacrificial altar for all spirits and piśācas.
The external sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) is established externally for the outer practice;
however, within the inner enclosures, the vehicle-pedestal (vāhanapīṭha) is said to be in the center. || 831 ||
One should prepare a flower-seat (puṣpapīṭha) in front of the central hall;
one should prepare a Gaṇa-seat (gaṇapīṭha) at the central and other established locations.
Outside the great boundary wall, however, the offering altar (balipīṭha) is established, provided with perfumes, flowers, and cooked rice, and equipped with incense and lamps. || 833 ||
Having performed worship at the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) accompanied by all the hosts of gods, [one worships] Vṛṣa, Yakṣeśāna, Mahākāla, and Gaṇa.
The gods and the sages, the ancestors, the Daityas and Dānavas,
the Yakṣas and the Rākṣasas, as well as the Nāgas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas— || 835 ||
The Kinnaras and Apsarases, as well as the Maruts and the Mātṛkās; Anāvṛṣṭi and the Gaṇas, and Rohiṇī and Gaṇarāva.
(From PDF 86, p.
736) O Prince, there are the hosts of Kūṣmāṇḍas and likewise eighteen hosts;
in the midst of the seat are the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, and Prajāpati. || 837 ||
One should worship all the bhūtas and piśācas outside the pedestal;
one should worship Vṛṣa in the eastern quarter and Īśa in the south.
Having worshipped Mahākāla in the west and the host of gods in the north with elephants and other offerings, one should cause the bali-offering to be given everywhere.
In the middle of the southern and northern regions, within the pericarp, there are three offerings for Prajāpati,
the gods, and the sages, respectively.
One should cause the ancestors and others to be offered [libations] starting from Nāga up to Īśāna;
having performed the sprinkling and cleansing, there should again be an auspicious re-worship.
One should cause perfumes, flowers, incense, and the sprinkling water to be offered separately;
and in every case, one should cause the *bali* offering to be given in the measure of a handful or half thereof.
One should cause the offering of incense and flowers with a mantra beginning with one's own name.
I shall now describe the procedure for the fire-ritual (agnikārya), which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
The rite of fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila).
These three—the foremost ones—are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara as their presiding deities.

Having prepared the sacrificial ground as before, listen now to the generation of the Śiva-fire: that which arises from a sun-crystal is the most excellent, as is that produced from the friction-sticks (*araṇi*). (845)
One should especially bring forth the Jātavedas fire of the Vedic tradition into a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even one made of clay.
Having cast that fire there while reciting the Śiva-mantra,
one should purify it with the Astra-mantra and enclose it with the Kavaca-mantra.
One should visualize [the deity] as having been rendered immortal by means of the primary seed-mantra;
then, whether in the fire-pit or on the sacrificial mound, one should place a seat provided with flowers. (848)
Having drawn a lotus provided with eight petals and a pericarp,
one should invoke therein Vāgīśī, the performer of the sacrifice, into its center.

One should then contemplate one's mother as being everywhere the source of all beings, having bathed after her menstrual period; thereafter, one should contemplate the god Maheśvara, who has three eyes and four arms.
One should also meditate there upon the goddess Vāgīśī, who is endowed with all the [auspicious] marks, adorned with every auspicious sign, and filled with joy.
Having strewn grass three times around that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should recite the Heart-mantra once;
then, facing the fire situated in the womb [of the pit], one should recite the "Sadyojāta" mantra while addressing the gods.
One should cast [the materials] while reciting the heart-mantra and collect them together;
afterwards, one should perform seven oblations while correctly reciting the heart-mantra. (853)
In the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), one should perform seven oblations to the Puruṣa;
but in the rite for ensuring a male child (puṃsavana), one should perform the fire-offering seven times with the Śiras mantra.
One should perform the birth-rites with the left [hand], offering seven oblations;
and in the rite of naming, one should sacrifice seven oblations with the heart-mantra.
In this manner, one should offer oblations with the *śiras* mantra during the rite of the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*);
and during the rites of the tonsure (*caula*) and the observances (*vrata*), one should offer seven times with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the Śiromantra, the Guru should perform the Samāvartana rite;
and for the sake of marriage, he should offer seven oblations with the Hṛdayamantra.
The offering of incense and lamps should be performed individually with the heart-mantra;
thus, through the sequence of oblations, the auspicious birth-rite of the Śiva-fire is accomplished. (858)
(From PDF 88, p.

738) Holding the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in the left hand, one should touch their tips with the tips of the *kuśa* grass held in the right hand, and touch their middles with the middles [of the grass]. (859)

In this manner, one should touch [the ladles] with their roots; thus occurs the purification of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as the vessel for clarified butter (*ājya-sthālī*), the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (*caru-sthālī*), and the *praṇītā* vessel.
One should wash [the vessel] with pure water while reciting the weapon-mantra;
one should fill the *praṇītā* vessel with water and place a *kūrca* grass-bundle therein.
One should sprinkle the entire collection of oblation materials with those waters;
having filled the vessel for the clarified butter with clarified butter, together with the *kūrca* grass-bundle.
Having thus circumambulated the fire three times from left to right,
one should then perform the placement of the clarified butter (ājya) in the western and northern directions.
Perform the sprinkling with the *sadyojāta* mantra, the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and the inspection with the *netra* mantra; then perform the placement of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

The placement of the enclosing sticks (paridhi) is auspicious when their tips point eastward and northward; one should worship the deities stationed at the enclosing sticks, beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna. || 865 ||
O Maheśvara, listen now to the meditation on the form of the auspicious fire (Śivāgni):
it has a single body, two faces, four horns, and two nostrils. (866)
Having three girdles, three feet, three eyes, and a triangular form;
wearing a sacred thread, with matted hair upon his crown, and surrounded by seven tongues of flame. || 867 ||
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, the one called Kṛṣṇā, the one named Suprabhā, Atiriktā, and Bahurūpā— these are proclaimed as the seven tongues.

Wearing a red turban and adorned with a red garland,

Circumambulation is of two kinds: the auspicious *śāntika* and the *pauṣṭika*.

Observing the vow of silence, conducting themselves with propriety, and contemplating Śiva in their thoughts,

Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, one should place the limbs in contact:
the head, hands, ears, chin, and both arms. (930)

having placed the head, the two hands, the two arms, and the two knees upon the ground. (931)

at its conclusion, one should perform the auspicious tāṇḍava dance which brings me joy. (932)
At that time, having uttered the song, the hymn, the Veda, and likewise the Jaya,
one should perform the embrace of the Liṅga, followed immediately by the Jñānamudrā.

thereafter, having worshipped the Bali-liṅga, one should deposit it upon the outer pedestal.
At the time of dawn, one should perform the Gāndhāra; at midday, the Tarkarāgin;
then, having performed the Kauśika, one should perform the auspicious Indula in the evening.
(From PDF 95, p. 747) || The Ritual of Initiation (Dīkṣāvidhi) ||
Now I shall describe the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*), which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments, pacifies untimely death, and increases longevity and health. (1)
That which is bestowed is indeed the state of Śiva, while the cage of sin is destroyed;
through the conjunction of bestowing and destroying, it is designated as *dīkṣā*.
On Mount Mahendra, Malaya, Vindhya, Paripātra, and Himālaya;
on the banks of the Gaṅgā, at sacred rivers, at the ocean, and even in a hermitage.
Either in a flower garden that is pure and near the Lord of Japa, or on a mountain peak, in a forest, in a cow-pen, in Śrīpura, or at a milk-tree; || 4 ||
In a Brahma-kuṇḍa, at a Kadamba tree, in the beautiful abode of a Guru,
especially in a temple or in a house with its entrance facing south.
One should designate the site for initiation at the root of the *kuṇḍa* tree.
The sequence for the site of initiation has been declared; now hear the rule for the time of initiation.
During the period of the northern solstice, in the bright fortnight on an auspicious day, as well as during the solstices, the equinoxes, and the eclipses of the moon and the sun. || 7 ||
In all months, on a day endowed with the teacher’s desire,
at an auspicious moment and a favorable astrological conjunction (lagna), one should perform the rite of initiation (dīkṣā).
Having first examined the qualities of his disciples for a full year, he should accept those endowed with virtue and avoid those who are devoid of virtue.
First, for the purpose of favoring the disciples, the wise teacher should cause them to take a tooth-stick;
then, having performed the ritual bath according to the previously described procedure.
The pavilion (maṇḍapa), which embodies all the gods, is pure and fulfills all desires;
having performed the purification of the ground as before, one should perform the decoration of the pavilion.
(From *pdf* 96, p.
748) Listen now to the colors, scents, and tastes according to the sequence of the four castes:
the color of the Brāhmaṇas is white, while that of the Kṣatriyas is red. (12)
The color of the Vaiśyas is yellow, while that of the Śūdras is black;
the scent of clarified butter belongs to the Brāhmaṇas, and the scent of blood belongs to the kings (Kṣatriyas). 13.
For Vaiśyas it has the fragrance of a lotus, and for Śūdras the smell of alkaline ash;
they are sweet, astringent, bitter, and pungent, respectively.
From the Brāhmaṇa down to the Śūdra, these are the tastes of the sacrificial ground;
thus the sacrificial ground is endowed with the colors, fragrances, and tastes [of each class]. (15)
It was provided with four gates, adorned with four archways, equipped with canopies and banners, and decorated with garlands of *darbha* grass. || 16 ||
It was provided with garlands of banners, adorned with flower garlands, and surrounded by betel-nut trees, plantain trees, and strings of pearls. (17)
It was adorned in every direction with numerous sacrificial ladles (pālikās),
and it was encircled by three lines made either with lime or with ashes.
Having prepared auspicious parched grain, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice together with offerings of flowers, and having measured it well with an excellent cord, one should drive stakes all around.
To the west, there are pillars made of conch-shell and khadira wood, as well as apāmārga and campaka;
they are twelve finger-breadths in height and half of that in circumference.
The mandala, threefold in size and joined with thirty-two threads,
should have its threads drawn in sequence, starting from the east and ending in the north.
Having stretched a cord from the southwest (Nairṛta) to the northeast (Īśa), and from the southeast (Āgneya) to the northwest (Vāyu) corner, one should then prepare an auspicious circular mandala.
Furthermore, one should draw an eight-petaled [lotus] with white and reddish dust; the pericarp with yellow-colored [dust], and the filaments with orange-colored [dust]. (23) (PDF 97, p. 749)
Its root and tip are white, and its petals are described as being of a white color; it should be the size of a lotus-hand, while the pericarp (karṇikā) is four finger-breadths in measure.
One should measure the lotus twice over according to the rule in detail;
on each door, there shall be three lines outside the lotus.
The measurement for the three parts outside the lotus is half of that half-lotus measurement;
at each interval at the edge of the lotus, listen now to the sequence of colors in the center.
It is red-colored in the east, black-colored in the south,
white-colored in the west, and has the luster of gold in the north.
In the southeast it is fire-colored, in the southwest it is blue-colored;
in the northwest it should be smoke-colored, and in the northeast it is white-colored. || 28 ||
One should draw a ninefold tree of nine colors outside the lotus;

With precious powder, one should draw the lines for the doors and other features;
with green powder on the outside, one should apply the three colors in their proper sequence.
One should have the primary ornamentation and the secondary embellishments drawn with white pigment, using a paste of rice and wheat flour well-mixed with powdered pearls. (31)
One should place powdered ruby and blue pigment in the center;
likewise, one should apply yellow powder in the southeast and blue powder there as well.
In the southwest, one should especially prepare powdered go-meda;
in the west, powdered pearl; and in the northwest, powdered vaidūrya.
In the north, it should be the color of coral; in the northeast, powdered ruby;
and [the colors] of minerals and flowers, as well as *brahmapuṣpa* and blue lotuses. (34)
With *dhurdhūra* flowers, large *bṛhatī* blossoms, and leaves of the *nandyāvarta*,
and with the colors of turmeric and fine rice for the center and the directions starting from the northeast (Īśāna).
And with these same colors, one should draw nine trees on the exterior:
the *kalpa*, the *bilva*, the *śamī*, the *vaṭa* tree, and the *campaka*.
One should place the Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Punnāga, and Candana trees in nine positions;

These petals, in sequence, as well as the great mandala itself,

thirty-two, one thousand, or eight hundred [squares].
Having thus laid out the sequence of petals, the circle of knowledge (jñānamaṇḍala) is described.
The maṇḍala is said to be of three kinds; therefore, hear now the procedure for the hand [maṇḍala]. || 40 ||
Likewise, eight *reṇus* make one *aṣṭa*; eight [of those] make a *keśa*, and eight [of those] make an *alikhya*.
Eight *yūkas* make one *yava*, and eight *yavas* make one finger (*aṅguli*). Two fingers make one *tālaka*. || 41 ||
Two tālas shall constitute one hasta; O Maheśvara, I shall now describe the measurements:
it may be one hasta, two hastas, or even four hastas.
It may be five, eight, or ten cubits, or likewise sixteen cubits; it may also be twenty cubits or twenty-five cubits.
The mandala should thus be thirty-two cubits; one should not construct it larger than that.
Once the mandala has been made and worshipped, one should perform the worship of Śiva in its center.

751) One should cause to be offered fragrance, flowers, lamps, and incense to the imperishable one who stands facing south, situated in the midst of all the gods. (45)

Having performed the ritual rinsing (ācāma) according to the rules while meditating upon Vīreśa and reciting [his name],

Having recited that mantra one hundred times, he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be proclaimed there;

One should bind it on the right hand with the mantra "viśvektātā";

One should cause the ashes to be offered with the mantra "bṛhatsāma";

Oṃ, salutations to Śambhu, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul;
salutations to the Auspicious One, whose form is the universe, the Lord of Dreams.
Having recited this mantra one hundred times, one should dwell at night before Śiva.
At that time, having meditated upon the form of the Guru as the Lord of the South (Dakṣiṇanāyaka), || 54 ||
For the sake of pacifying obstacles, one should prepare five jars,
equipped with threads, cloths, and gems, prepared as previously described.

752) One should consecrate the central temple with the Īśāna mantra.
Then, one should place [the mantras] starting from Puruṣa and ending with Vāma in the directions beginning with the east and ending with the north. (56)
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, and having meditated upon the one whose nature is Brahman,
one should utter the heart-mantra and present the food offering and other gifts.
Having thus formed this resolution according to the rules, one should perform the morning bath;
then one should report the dream, whether auspicious or inauspicious, as well as any evil dreams.
One should perform the collection [of materials] for auspicious rites and the fire-oblation (homa) for inauspicious ones;
having washed both feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules. || 59 ||
With a garment of fine *dukūla* silk, or a variegated silken cloth, or else with a new cloth made of cotton. || 60 ||
Reciting the Netra-mantra ten times, the teacher, facing north and remaining composed, should bind [the cloth] over the eyes of the disciple. (61)
Having recited the Puruṣa mantra, one should take up the flower;
with the Īśāna mantra, however, one should offer a handful of flowers.
Having performed three circumambulations, one should cause [the flower] to be offered with the Vāma mantra;
on whichever cloth the flower falls, the name [of the disciple] shall be of that same nature.
Listen now to the name, the lineage, the scripture, the sphere of activity, the jewel-tree, the Śaiva principle, and the time, according to the sequence of the forms and powers. 64.
Īśāna, Vaktreya, Ghorabrahma, Sadyojāta, Rudra, and Vāma—these nine names of Ahaṃkāra are thus declared. (65)
One should utter the names of the Brāhmaṇas ending with Śiva, those of the Rudras ending with Gaṇa, and for the sequence starting from Sadyojāta in direct order, the names ending with Śakti. (66)
Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Bhāradvāja, Jaimini, Agastya, Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, Parāśara, and Romaśa (67).
The Śiva-sūtra, the Nada-sūtra, the Śakti-sūtra, the Brahma-sūtra, the Bindu-sūtra, the Viṣṇu-sūtra, and thereafter the Vāyavya-sūtra. || 68 ||
Soma-sūtra, Mahāsūtra, and the nine sūtras—these indeed are the Unborn;
Śiva is the crest-jewel, the bliss of light, Sāvitrī, and the possessor of true qualities.
The sky and the pervasive one—these are remembered as the ninefold spheres of perception:
the *kalpa*, the *bilva*, the *śamī*, the banyan tree (*vaṭa*), and the *campaka*. (70)
The Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Punnāga, and sandalwood trees that are newly sprouted;
as well as ruby, pearl, topaz, and sapphire. (71)
Vaiḍūrya, gomeda, gāruḍa, pravālaka,
and sphāṭika— these are proclaimed as the nine kinds of gems.
The first is the Śaiva [Tantra] of the Upper [Region], the second is the Ādi-Śaiva, the third is the Anādi-Śaiva, and the fourth is the Anu-Śaiva. || 73 ||

The fifth is the intermediate [Śaiva], while the sixth is the Mixed Śaiva (Miśraśaiva). The seventh would be the Differentiated Śaiva (Bhedaśaiva), and the eighth is the Quality-based Śaiva (Guṇaśaivaka).
The ninth is Ājñāśaiva; thus the Śaiva [tattvas] are ninefold in sequence:
the Śiva-tattva, the Vahni-tattva, and then that consisting of Śakti and Jñāna.
The reality of the non-dual, attribute-less [Brahman], which consists of the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva—these nine principles have been declared;
now hear of the nine Kālas in their proper order. (76)
At the time of creation he is Vidhātṛ; at the time of maintenance he is Keśava;
at the time of dissolution he is Rudra; and at the time of enjoyment he is Maheśvara. (77)
(From PDF 102, p.
754) At the time of yoga, however, it is Sādākhya; at the time of knowledge, it is Binduka;

At the time of Śiva, however, there is a distinction: thereafter, in sequence, [he is] the form of Īśāna, then the form of Śiva, the form of Śakti, the essence of Nāda, and the form of Bindu. || 79 ||
The bodies of Sadāśiva, Maheśāna, Rudra, Keśava, and Vedhas are said to be ninefold; now hear also of their Śaktis.

The primordial power (Ādi-śakti), the power of action (Kriyā-śakti), the power of light (Jyotiḥ-śakti) whose nature consists of the qualities (Guṇa), the power of knowledge (Jñāna-śakti), the power of victory (Jayā-śakti), and the power known as Yogānandā. || 81 ||
The powers of differentiation, the substratum, the self, and energy are recorded as being ninefold;
the distinctions such as Name and so forth have been fully declared—now hear the sequence of the letters of the gates.
The southern gate is the best for the four castes in their respective order;
however, O Maheśvara, the eastern gate is highly recommended for Brāhmaṇas.
The southern gate is for the Kṣatriyas, while the auspicious northern gate is for the Vaiśyas;

one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the five Brahmans and the six limbs as previously described.
Having recited the root mantra once with the heart-mantra, he should gaze upon that withdrawal (saṃhāra) situated in the five locks of hair upon the disciple's head.
Having observed the place of duality, one should cause the hand of Śiva to be placed there,
having properly proclaimed the rule (samaya) in the presence of the God of gods.
One should always remain at the feet of Śiva, which are beyond reproach according to all scriptures; one must not even step over the shadow of the Ācārya or of the elder Liṅgas.
One should avoid association with a woman who has not been initiated;
one should not consume the remains of offerings (nirmālya); and one should not revile those smeared with ashes. (103.89)
One should initiate the disciple along with his kinsmen and his wife;
having thus received them, one should afterwards perform the fire sacrifice (homa). || 90 ||
Having blocked all the gates of the body at the seat (pīṭha) and likewise restrained the senses, the state of blocking sound is known as the organ of hearing. 91.
