One should have it made there with copper, having a circumference of twelve finger-breadths;
its tip is proclaimed to have a circumference of twenty-four finger-breadths.
Measuring ten finger-breadths up to eighteen finger-breadths, it is declared to be of three types: superior, middling, and inferior. (49)

It should be made according to the *adhamāṅgula* measure; one should have it constructed using the *mānāṅgula*. The best [size] is one cubit (*hasta*) in length, provided with five wooden planks (*phalaka*).
That which is twenty finger-breadths in length is prescribed as the best;
that which is eighteen finger-breadths in length and ten finger-breadths in width [is also excellent]. || 51 ||
Having performed the intermediate rite, one should then prepare the inferior one;
it should be one cubit in measure and four finger-breadths in width.
Then, having made the length of the staff three parts, one-fifth [of that],
and then seven parts, one should arrange [the proportions].
With the invocation and consecration, the best [mandala] is nine cubits;
the middling is seven cubits, and the lowest is six cubits.
Having thus performed [the rite] according to the rule, as well as the binding of the cloth-band, [this is] the supreme [measure] of five tālas. || 55 ||
Having made a triangle elongated, equal to the two tails... (56)
The tail should be half the width [of the body], or two tails, or three tails. || 57 ||
The form of the banner is proclaimed to be endowed with these characteristics;
on the northern side of the bull, in a place smeared with auspicious cow-dung, [it should be placed]. (58)
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) made of eight droṇas of śāli rice for the feet; having placed one's foot upon it, one should draw a bull and other such figures.
A battle-axe, a skull-topped staff, a noose, and likewise a trident;
a parasol, two lamps, and likewise chowries on both sides. (60)
One should meditate upon the white bull, adorned with all ornaments, seated in the lotus posture;
its two horns are proclaimed to be red.
All the hooves likewise raised up, with a radiance like that of the rising sun;
one should draw a bull, whether black or white, and auspicious.
The mounts of the eight world-protectors are positioned in their respective directions;
it is endowed with nine banners and has the form of the elephant of Indra’s peak.
One should place a goat in the eastern regions, a buffalo in the southern region,
a lion in the southwestern region, and likewise a crocodile in the western region.
A deer is prescribed for the northwestern direction, a horse for the northern, and a bull for the northeastern; this [arrangement] is on the right side.
Having written [the mantra] and performed the rites as before, one should bathe and perform worship;
specifically, the worship of the root deity with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is auspicious.
(From PDF 120, p.
772) One should worship the wonderful Lord Dakṣiṇeśvara with special care;
the most excellent of preceptors should worship Him according to the extent of his available wealth. 67.
A square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) made of eight droṇas of śāli rice, with a width of two cubits and a height of four finger-breadths, [should be prepared] with the rice. 68.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with a line of white rice grains,
one should subsequently draw the four corners and other parts using water and sesame seeds.
Having established the *kūrca* seat and consecrated the auspicious sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*),
one should place upon the *kūrca* a water-pot (*kumbha*) made of gold, silver, or copper.
Alternatively, it may be made of copper, very firm and of auspicious form,
or else made of gold, silver, or even cotton.
Having wrapped it with thread according to the rules, one should place it upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
filled with scented water and provided with the five jewels.
One should place these five jewels— ruby, pearl, lapis lazuli, sapphire, and coral— into the bull-vessel.
One should insert the mantra of Īśa with the seed-syllable of Mūlaprakṛti;
having wrapped it with a cloth, one should offer fragrance and flowers. || 74 ||
Having worshipped the bull upon the jar with the root mantra,
the knower of mantras should place the banner to the south and likewise the flagstaff to the north.
One should cause the previously mentioned offerings to be presented to the world-protectors of the eight directions;
then, having performed a gradual circumambulation, one should take refuge in the temple.
Having established [the deity] in the pavilion as before, one should cause fragrant flowers to be offered.
O Maheśvara, listen as I describe the sequence for the installation of the banner. (77)
The location for the banner is in the middle of the door’s sacrificial pedestal;
it should be two cubits, three cubits, or even one cubit in measure. (78)
One should withdraw [the deity] with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) or likewise install the water-pot (kumbha).
Therein, one should install the image (mūrti) with the staff-mantra (daṇḍa), and therein the staff (daṇḍaka).
One should make the altar (vedikā) smooth; the altar is prescribed to be three cubits [in width]. Its height should be three tālas, and one should place the girdle (mekhalā) upon it.
Having planned it higher and higher, the height should be one palm (tāla) less;
specifically, the width should be half of that height. || 81 ||
All the girdles (mekhalās) are said to be square on all sides;
in this manner one should fashion the most excellent of altars (vedikās). || 82 ||
Above that, one should fashion a structure joined with leaves, one tāla in height,
either circular, square, or in the shape of a lotus.
It should be smeared with cow dung, pure, adorned with powdered flour, provided with three lines of ash, and decorated with white flowers. || 84 ||
There, one should cause the Brahmins to recite the *puṇyāha* formula and then honor them;
[one should set up] a banner eight cubits long, joined with bells and adorned with garlands. 85.
One should cause eight flowers to be offered to the world-protectors of the eight directions with the ten-syllable mantra, while binding the cords in due order.
Having uttered the five-syllable mantra during the rite of erecting the banner,
one should worship the vehicle there with the seed-syllable beginning with the first vowel.
Having raised up the bull-pitcher,
one should likewise [establish] the temple, as well as the village, the city, and the port, with the mantra of Dakṣeśvara.
Alternatively, one should slowly perform a circumambulation of the capital city,
taking recourse to the site of the banner and accompanied by the installation of the sacrificial post (yaṣṭi). (89)
One should bind the smooth noose with the mantra beginning with the syllable Oṃ;
one should then fix the binding of the banners facing toward the temple.
There, the beautiful eastern banner was described as being endowed with all auspicious characteristics and adorned with every kind of ornament.
He was clad in white garments, anointed with white sandalwood paste,
endowed with the virtues of white garlands, and possessed a white sacred thread.
Having worshipped it in due order, one should sprinkle with the Astra-mantra a new cloth tied around the head and provided with a waist-thread.

O Maheśvara, one should offer rice cooked with cow products (*gaulānna*) and milk-rice (*kṣīrānna*) that has been thoroughly stirred; that food is for the sake of the success of recitation and for the sake of enjoyment. (94)
Having worshipped [the deity] at the base of the flagstaff in that manner, one should place a bull-shaped vessel there;
one should wrap the staff with cloth and cover it with beautiful tips of *darbha* grass.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should offer incense, lamps, and the like;
thereafter, one should worship during the three junctions of the day and offer milk-rice (pāyasa).
I shall describe the deities of the banners: Bhṛṅgīśa, Nandikeśvara, Mahākāla, and Caṇḍeśa—one should worship them upon the altar and other such locations. (97)
The staff (daṇḍa) has Śiva as its presiding deity; the stick (yaṣṭi) is the goddess Sarasvatī;
the plowshare (phālaka) has five deities; and the hollow part (suṣira) consists of Pārvatī.
The rope has Takṣaka as its presiding deity; the foot has Māruta (the Wind-god) as its deity;
the bull has Īśa (Śiva) as its deity; and the trident has Jyotsnādhidaivata (the presiding deity of moonlight) as its deity. || 99 ||
The axe has Caṇḍa as its deity; the two lamps have Śiva as their deity;
the fly-whisks have the Moon and Sun as their lords; and the bell has the Bull as its deity. (100)
The wise one, having established the deities beginning with Bhṛṅgīśa in the eight directions, should worship them with their respective names and likewise worship the sounds. 101.
At the time of hoisting the banner, one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara and honor all the gods in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
In the evening, at an auspicious moment, one should begin the beating of the drum;
one should prepare a square mandala in front of the pavilion.

One should prepare the sacrificial ground as before; there, having worshipped the nine Śaktis in their proper order upon the petals of an eight-petaled [lotus] made with eight *droṇas* of rice, || 104 ||

One should offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya) while reciting each deity's respective name, preceded by the utterance of the root mantra conjoined with the syllable Om (praṇava). || 105 ||
Then, having placed a drum in the center of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should worship it;
the drum has Skanda as its presiding deity, and its touch belongs to the deity Vāyu.
But the sound is joined with Pārvatī; that substance has Śambhu as its presiding deity.
The leather thong is Vāsukī, and the two bracelets are the Moon and the Sun. (107)
The wise one, having worshipped the seven mother-kīlas with fragrant substances and other offerings, [dedicating them] to the deity Praharaskanda, using the heart-mantra. || 108 ||
Having recited the *Nandi-mantra*, the Guru should strike the drum;
he should then strike the musical instruments with the mantra "Tatpuruṣa. (109)
Śivatāla, Dhātritāla, combined with Murārītāla, Vṛṣatāla, Śūlatāla, Kaṭatāla, and Vitālaka. (110)
(From PDF 124, p.
776) At the boundary of the village, the army, accompanied by conchs and trumpets, and attended by singers, musicians, and dancers, [should worship] Brahmā and Īśāna. || 111 ||
One should offer a bali-oblation to the gods by their respective names, using these substances: sesame seeds, powdered turmeric, and king’s-lentil flour soaked in curd.
Having performed the circumambulation slowly, one should thereafter take refuge in the temple;
there, one should perform worship during the three junctions of the day, beginning with the invocation and ending with the ritual bath at the sacred ford.
One should worship the deity of the banner, adorned with all ornaments,
for the sake of the festival and the sacred bathing place, from the limbs down to the minor parts and their respective pacifications.
The seven-limbed, the four-limbed, and that which is proclaimed as having seven secondary limbs;
the flagstaff and so forth, the tree, and the sacrificial offering (bali) are all established. 115.
The protective rite (rakṣā), the staff (daṇḍa), the ceremonial bath (snapana), and the festival (utsava) are proclaimed as the constituent parts [of the ritual].
In this context, there are also the ḍokāra and rathāṃ, as well as the yantra and the raṅga.
There were mechanical temples and likewise mechanical pavilions;
there were mechanical trees, mechanical dancers, and mechanical guards.
There were horse-machines, lion-machines, and likewise elephant-machines;
bull-machines, spirit-machines, and likewise god-machines. || 118 ||
One should cause to be made various and variegated peacock-feather fans, as well as diverse types of insignia, umbrellas of many forms, and chowries. || 119 ||
One should not defile the temple from above or below;
having constructed a very beautiful water-shed (prapā) in the northeast direction of the temple.
One should decorate the sacrificial hall as beautifully as possible with curtains, garlands, and so forth;
then, one should construct it in the northeast or the southeast.
(From PDF 125, p.
777) One should have a pavilion constructed there, provided with sixteen pillars, measuring ten cubits, nine cubits, or even seven cubits. 122.
It is provided with four gates, adorned with four archways, furnished with garlands of *darbha* grass, and beautified by canopies and banners. (123)
One should fashion an altar in the center using one-ninth part [of the area];
it should be one cubit in height, pleasing to the eye, and resembling the surface of a mirror.
Then, in the middle of the altar, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with auspicious rice grains—
either six, five, or four *droṇas*— according to the prescribed rule.
Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce a "holy day" (puṇyāha), one should also have them chant auspicious sounds;
then, during the night of the festival, there shall be a great worship of the Lord of the South.
One should perform the worship of the image with a great offering of oblations;
and at the commencement of the festival, one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) as previously described. || 127 ||

Having established [the vessel] in the center of the altar, provided with the five jewels, endowed with the characteristics of a water-pot (kumbha), furnished with a tuft of grass (kūrca), and wrapped in cloth. || 128 ||
In the midst of that, joined with sandalwood water, he is seated upon a lotus;
he has four arms, three eyes, holds a trident in his hand, and wears matted hair.
The god bears the crescent moon, is adorned with serpent ornaments, wears a golden sacred thread, and has rings set with the nine gems. || 130 ||
During the festival, one should worship Lord Śambhu, the consecrated Lord of Sacrifice (Yāgeśvara).
The Vardhanī vessel, joined with the Kūrca, is established on his left side.
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with all ornaments,
she holds the gestures of fearlessness and knowledge, as well as a lotus and a goad.
One should place the two Paritoṣṭas there, together with the Vidyeśvaras;
then follow the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), and thereafter water with gems. (133)
One should place eight jars, beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna, containing flower-water, sesame-water, barley-water, and fragrant water.
One should worship Indra and the other deities, endowed with all their characteristic marks; one should fashion the ten weapons either out of metal or wood.
One should worship all those forms of the deities, with their heads adorned by weapons, one after another in sequence outside the water-jars.
In the directions starting from the east, the weapons such as the vajra are placed in clockwise order;
the deity of the wheel is in the north, while the deity of the lotus is in the south.
One should worship the forms of the eight auspicious symbols outside the altar;
one should worship the auspicious trident in the direction of the wind (the northwest) at the three junctions of the day.
One should generate the Śiva-fire in the east and worship it auspiciously as before—the God who has three eyes, four arms, and is adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament. (139)
One should offer oblations into the seven tongues of fire to the embodiment of sacrifice who has received the offerings;
a multitude of fuel-sticks with the Heart-mantra, and clarified butter with the Puruṣa-mantra. (140)
One should offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora mantra and parched grains (lāja) with the Aghorāstra mantra;
one should offer groats (saktu) with the Vāma mantra and milk indeed with the Sadyojāta mantra.
O Maheśvara, having offered barley with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, white mustard seeds with the *sadyojāta-mantra*, and molasses with the *Śiva-gāyatrī-mantra*. (142)

One should offer sesame seeds with the *Mīśāna* mantra and black gram with the *Udbhaṇa* mantra; at the end of each substance, one should offer the *Vyāhṛtis*, and then it is declared that the names of the Rudras shall be sacrificed.
(From PDF 127, p.
779) Listen now to the names of the fourteen Rudras in their proper order:
Dhūmayāna, Bhūta, Vasudhā, Taru, and Kalā. (144)
The *rakṣanetra*, the *avicchedasāman*, and likewise the *adinam*; the *jñānapuṣpa* and so forth, the *gīti* and so forth, the seven *rudras*, and the fourteen. 145.
Each [of these] is eightfold, and at the end there are one hundred and twelve;
this is the smoke-obscuration (*dhūmāvaraṇa*).
The enclosure of the vehicles of Dhūmrarudra, Bhūtanīlarudra, Pāśarudra, Nāśarudra, Ājasthirarudra, and Yānarudra.
Yānarudra, Ghorarudra, Vīrarudra, Somarudra, Vāsarudra, Keśarudra, Śrīrudra, Mahārudra, Vararudra.
The enclosure of the spirits (bhūtāvaraṇa).
The enclosure of the Vasus consists of Bhūtarudra, Vāsarudra, Vāyurudra, Sparśarudra, Tvakkarudra, Īśarudra, Nāgarudra, Galarudra, Agnirudra, and Vasvadhārudra.
Vasudhārudra, Śrīrudra, Cakṣurudra, Ātmarudra, Rasarudra, Jihvārudra, Śabdarudra, Ati-atistha Rudra, Taruṇāvaraṇa,
Taruṇarudra, Śikhārudra, Jyotsnārudra, Khararudra, Satyarudra, Manorudra, Śubharudra.
The enclosure of Aṇḍarudra and Kāla.
O Kālarudra, O Mahārudra, may there be auspiciousness and a three-day festival for Śiva. || 146 ||
(From PDF 128, p.
780) A devoted man should perform the rite for a single day as prescribed for Śiva, offering pure food mixed with curd, along with sweetmeats and cakes. (147)
Fruit mixed with molasses brings satisfaction and auspiciousness to the Gaṇas;
likewise, fruit mixed with powdered turmeric and rice with parched grain flour [is pleasing]. || 148 ||
He [offered] that which was mixed with curd, beginning with flowers, which brings delight to all beings,
along with bilva leaves, tips of kuśa grass, and rice mixed together.
An offering of female deer is said to consist of plantain fruit;
likewise, *indravallī*, turmeric, and *priyaṅgu* combined with clarified butter [are offered]. (150)
On the fourth day, the offering for Śakra is prescribed;
it consists of lotus flowers, turmeric, parched grain, and milk-rice (pāyasa). || 151 ||
On the fifth day, one should give auspicious food that brings pleasure to Brahmā:
rice mixed with jaggery and ghee, combined with the fruit of the bṛhatī plant.
On the sixth day, the Vaiṣṇava bali is prescribed to be offered;
it should consist of kṛsarā rice with clarified butter, combined with coconut fruits.
Accompanied by coconut fruits, it is auspicious and pleasing to Rudra;
likewise, milk-rice mixed with curd and combined with plantain fruits [is offered]. (154)
On the eighth day, one should offer that which is auspicious and pleasing to Īśa,
consisting of five kinds of cooked rice along with cakes, and completely filled with clarified butter.
On the ninth day, one should offer the auspicious gift known as Sādākhya, which bestows delight;
it consists of rice mixed with jaggery, milk-rice, and pure food filled with ghee.
On the tenth day, one should offer auspicious food that brings delight to Bindu;
it should consist of pure rice mixed with molasses and filled with milk. (157)
On the eleventh day, the auspicious gift that brings pleasure to Gaurī should be given;
on the twelfth day, the auspicious gift that brings pleasure to Śiva should be given. (158)
Alternatively, sugar, curd, and ghee mixed with pure boiled rice is auspicious and brings great delight to all the gods. (159)
Having performed worship especially with the respective mantras, one should cause [the gift] to be given—either a *droṇa*, or half of that, or half of that again, or half of that once more. || 160 ||
One should offer the bali-oblation separately for each, using portions the size of a hen's egg;
one should especially decorate both the village and the city.
The streets were cleared of grass and other debris, free from depressions and elevations, swept clean, purified by being sprinkled with drops of water. (162)
Having recited the syllable-mantra (varṇamantra), one should sprinkle [the area] with pure water,
as well as with many banners and sky-flags (ākāśadhvaja).
With *kramuka* nuts and plantains, with clusters of flaming lamps, and with many full water-jars adorned with variegated cloths and other ornaments. || 164 ||
One should adorn all the houses with garments, fragrant perfumes, and garlands;
then, for the sake of the festival, one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) as was done in former times.
With cymbals, kahalas, and jhallaris, abounding with incense and lamps, accompanied by peacock-feather fans, and with those reciting hymns and the *Aṅgamantras*. || 166 ||
In the center of the golden stage, there should be a trident and a liṅga;
likewise, all those present should bow their heads to the ground before the presence of the yantra.
He [the officiant] should be adorned with all ornaments, wearing a turban and an upper garment.
The teacher, accompanied by his disciples and surrounded by Brahmins, should especially offer the bali-oblation from Brahmā to Īśāna. (169) (pdf 130, p. 782)
The tip of the trident has the form of a *kalā*, while its base has the form of Rudra;
thus, the placement (*nyāsa*) and worship (*ārādhana*), both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*), are performed in due order.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers the sacrificial materials together with the deities beginning with Vajra and ending with Padmaka, one should then assume the form of Rudra.
At the conclusion of the festival, one should go forth adorned with all ornaments.
Equipped with various weapons, they arrived;
at their end were those mounted on elephants, and at their end, those whose vehicles were horses.
At the end of that, they are mounted on mechanical devices and attended by celestial women;
at the end of those are horse-machines, and at the end of those are elephant-machines.
At its end is the maṇṭapa-mechanism, and at its end are the ox-mechanisms;
in the center are the temple-machines for the deities, accompanied by dance and song. (175)
The first is seated on a comfortable throne; the second has a bull as his vehicle;
the third is the destroyer of Tripura; and the fourth is the moon-crested one. (176)
The fifth is Ardhanārīśa, the sixth is Hariharardha;
the seventh shall be Bhikṣamūrti, and the eighth is Kālanāśana. || 177 ||
The ninth is Kāladahana; the tenth is Para-kalyāṇasundara;
the eleventh is Liṅgastha; and the twelfth is Sadāśiva. || 178 ||
The thirteenth, however, is the Lord of Dance (Nṛtteśa), endowed with all ornaments;
he is [mounted] upon a stage, or a palanquin, or a chariot, or else an elephant. (179)
At the end of that [are] the Pāśupatas; at the end of that, those of the Great Vow (Mahāvrata); at the end of that, the Mahāśaivas; and at the end of that, the Brāhmaṇas in due order. (180)
At its end were all the Brahmins; at its end were the servants of the Siddhas;
at its end were all the singers; and at its end were the dancing women. || 181 ||
Accompanied by the Goddess Śakti, the lords proceed at its end with hundreds [of attendants], surrounded on all sides by throngs of women adorned with every ornament.
With various flowers, banners, and parasols, accompanied by various chowries, joined by various beings, and bearing various kahalas. || 183 ||
It was adorned everywhere with lamps on the three folds [of the belly], especially with mechanical lamps, hand-lamps, and staff-lamps.
The fierce leader deity should go behind [the procession] from all sides;
at its end, one should cause it to be proclaimed there, accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
With kettledrums, mṛdaṅgas, cymbals, bherīs, dundubhis, and jhallakas;
with paṇavas, jhallaris, lutes, kinnara-flutes, and reed-pipes. || 186 ||
One should especially cause it to be proclaimed both in front and behind;
at its conclusion, the Vaiśyas and Śūdras should proceed, joined with silent recitation (japa). || 187 ||
At the end of all those [periods] are those in the form of elephants;
then there are the old, the children, the young, the eunuchs, and those who enjoy worldly pleasures.
At the end of that [procession], the servant-devotees should proceed slowly and gradually, those who follow the deity with their innermost selves absorbed in him. (189)
At every step, men obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
they are liberated from all sins and shall attain the state of Shiva. || 190 ||
In this manner, one should perform circumambulation of either a village or a city,
specifically visualizing the sacred seats (pīṭhas) extending from Indra to Īśāna. (191)
One should offer an oblation to Kṣetrapāla at the Dhānyaśālā on the Sarasvatī;
to Prajāpati in the Maṇḍapa, and to the deity Nandin at the Gopura.
One should place Vāsukī on the rampart, and Indra and the other deities [on the walls];
Śrīdevī at the royal gate, and Naṭeśvarī in the assembly hall.
These are the presiding deities of the east for Āditya and Mahendra;
the Great Goddess is in the garden, and Gomukhī is in the cow-pen.
In the place of Durgā, however, there is a distinction: she is the primordial goddess of the cosmic egg;
in the place of Rudra she has the form of Rudra, and in the place of Viṣṇu she is Vaiṣṇavī.
Vāgdevī is at the site of Brahmā, and Manonmanī is at the site of the Guru;
the deities of the Moon are at the pond, and likewise Śiva is at the well.
At Valmīka, he is Nāgarāja; on Parvata, he is Parameśvarī;
at Citrasthāna, he is the Gandharvas; and at Nadīnām, he is Karuṇālayī.
In the place of the elephant, Vighneśa; in the place of the horse, the Aśvins;
in the place of the cow, Pārvatī; and in the cremation ground, Piśācikā. (198)
One should cause the bali offering to be given to these deities by their own names, along with flowers and boiled rice, or flowers, parched grain flour, fried grains, and sesame seeds. (199)
One should offer the combined substance of all [these fruits] under their own names:
the mango, the *kelī* fruit, and the plantain fruit. (200)
One should cause parched grain, cakes, rice with jaggery, and betel leaf to be offered;
this pacifies the suffering of poverty and bestows the fulfillment of all desires. || 201 ||
(From PDF 133, p.

785) O Lord of the Earth, by the mere offering of a bali-oblation, one goes gradually to the abode of Śiva; having gone to the temple, one should cast the bali upon the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha). || 202 ||
Having washed his feet, he should enter toward the temple;
meanwhile, the Lord remains in the pavilion together with all the hosts of gods.
The great sounds of mṛdaṅgas and other instruments were situated in the eastern direction,
while the dancers and the drummers were stationed in the south.
The singer and the flute-player are stationed in the north;
the teacher is in the eastern quarter, and the king is in the west. (205)
On both sides of the god stood female attendants;
and especially before the god, there was dancing, singing, and rhythmic accompaniment.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and cause celestial women to hold ashes,
flowers, lamps, as well as wonderful umbrellas and chowries.
One should place a mirror and a golden pitcher upon a three-legged stand;
then one should offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya), as well as flowers upon the head.
Having placed unbroken rice grains on the head, one should especially offer fragrant scents;
then one should give water for sipping (ācamana) and cause incense and lamps to be presented.
One should offer a lamp and a veil, performing circumambulation above the head;
at the conclusion of that, one should cause ashes to be given and then show a mirror.
Having had courtesans carry lamps accompanied by musical instruments,
or having placed them upon a seat, one should cast them outside the walls.
At the beginning of the festival, at the start of the first night, one should place the auspicious thread (kautuka) upon all;
indeed, on the first night of the festival, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
(From PDF 134, p.
786) One should subsequently cause the five-colored oblation to be offered into the five faces;
one should give milk-rice (pāyasa) to the eastern face, and rice with ghee (ghṛtodaṇa) to the southern face. || 213 ||
In the west, rice with jujube (gulānna), and likewise in the north, rice with turmeric;
in the upward-facing [direction], pure rice—such is the five-colored food offering (naivedya).
One should perform worship at the three junctions of the day (trisandhyā), together with the retinue,
as well as the image, the *golaka*, the trident, and the deity of the sacrifice.
The wise king should perform worship at the three junctions of the day for the prosperity of his kingdom;
at the conclusion of that, he should perform sacrifice, offerings, oblations, and circumambulation. (216)
At the three junctions of the day, one should present water for the feet, water for sipping, the respectful offering (arghya), fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings. || 217 ||
In this very manner, one should perform all the rites day after day;
however, for one who has died previously, one should first undertake the hunt.
By the power of the commencement of battle, one should circumambulate the village clockwise;
one should especially bind the protective thread (kautuka) on the boundary at night.
Having recited the heart-mantra over a thread made of gold, silver, or even cotton, one should there cause the declaration of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be proclaimed.
I shall describe the sequence for the powder festival; listen thus, O Maheśvara.
On the western side of the temple, one should prepare a square area with rice grains.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there, provided with eight petals in its center;
one should then wash the mortar and pestle with the weapon-mantra (astramantra).

In the center of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), having placed the mortar upon a seat of the Praṇava and enveloping it with a cloth, one should worship it with scents, flowers, and other offerings.
One should cause it to be adorned with sprouts after having worshipped it in due order:
turmeric, uśīra, kuṣṭha, camphor, and sapichala. (224) [PDF 135, p. 787]
Having placed everything ground into powder in the center of the mortar, one should recite the Sadyojāta mantra and worship Maheśvara. || 225 ||
The teacher should perform the rite of powdering first; then the king; after that, the learned Brahmins; and finally, the devoted people. (226)
Let courtesans adorned with new garments and ornaments attend upon Rudra and the others;
one should make [the area] beautiful with sprouts and provided with perfumes and flowers. (227)
Dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the application of cosmetic powders [should be performed] repeatedly;
[these are assigned to] the Liṅga, the mirror, the trident, the image, and the retinue.
Having made an anointing with oil, the preceptor should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara and cause the powder to be given to the king and his devotees.
Then, one should cause powder mixed with oil to be offered by all castes, accompanied by the sounds of conchs, kahalas, kettledrums, and other musical instruments. (230)
Having caused the Brahmins to proclaim auspicious blessings with words of well-being and prosperity,
he should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there, adorned with an eight-petaled lotus.
Having placed the trident there, one should set down the ritual jars at its tip; and having established Maheśvara, the deity of sacrifice, to the north of the trident.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should offer betel leaf;
one should prepare a mound of sand facing the image.
Having placed nine vessels that are very firm and comfortable in the northern region of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should further perform the purification of those vessels.
Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should then sprinkle them with water;
likewise, [one should sprinkle] the diamond (*vajra*), emerald (*marakata*), ruby (*padmarāga*), and sapphire (*nīlaka*). (235) (PDF 136, p. 788)
And one should place a pearl in the center of that, and arrange the five jewels;
having offered water for the feet in the eastern direction, one should offer water for sipping.
O Acyuta, one should then place the *arghya* vessel in the west and the *tīrtha* vessel in the north;
the vessel for scented water should be placed in the southeast and the vessel for fragrant water in the southwest.
In the northwest, the materials for smearing; in the northeast, the flowers;
and [the goddesses] Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Narmadā, and Sarasvatī. (238)
Having drawn forth the Sindhu, the Godāvarī, and the Kāverī— the sevenfold sacred sites—
from the center of the Bindu, one should place them within the fragrant waters.
One should worship, in sequence, those beginning with Anta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin in the jars;
one should also deposit the *kūrca* there, as well as the limbs and sub-limbs.
Having wrapped it with a cloth, one should place the *tulasī* there;
then, having worshipped it in due order with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth. || 241 ||
At the conclusion of the bathing, one should perform the offering of water for the feet (pādya) and offer it with the Sadyojāta mantra;
the water for sipping (ācamana) with the Puruṣa mantra, and the respectful offering (arghya) with the Īśāna mantra.
Afterwards, one should cause the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) to be offered with the five Brahma-mantras;
likewise, [the mantras] *ghṛtam bhakṣa* for the ghee-bath and *dadhikrāvṇo* for the curds.
One should perform the bathing of the image there in the middle of the river with milk using the *payasvat* mantra, and likewise with honey using the *madhuvātā* mantras. (244)
Then one should perform the ritual bath with the trident (śūla-snāna), as well as the protective thread (kautuka) and the two sacred sites (tīrthaka);
[these constitute] the great sacred site, the great subjugation, protection, and the destruction of enemies.
(See PDF 137, p. 788;
repeat page p. 789)
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, he should then enter the temple (page missing in PDF 138, p. 790).
They stood in the temple at the rear, according to their respective order. || 257 ||
The preceptor should worship [the deities] as before with garments, ornaments, flowers, and so forth;
then, having performed a circumambulation, he should worship the pure deities.
Thus, he who performs the festival of Śiva with supreme devotion rejoices in the world of Śiva, accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage. (259)
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause this great festival of Śiva to be performed according to the prescribed rules for the sake of the prosperity of the king and the kingdom. (260)
Listen to the rule for atonement as proclaimed in the Śivotsava-vidhi.
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the festival of Śiva in the Kriyāpāda of the Trisāhasrikā Saṃhitā of the Makuta Tantra.
(PDF 139, p.
791) Regarding the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*): "expiation" (*prāya*) is said to mean destruction, and "mind" (*citta*) is called "reconnection" (*sandhāna*).
But the mending of what has been destroyed is known as expiation (prāyaścitta). || 1 ||
I shall now declare the expiation beginning with plowing and ending with worship;
if there is a lapse in the time for worship, that twilight rite must be performed twice.
If one fails to perform the worship of a single twilight, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Brahma-mantra;
having offered milk-rice (pāyasa), one should then perform the worship of Śiva once again.
If the worship is deficient by one day, the bathing with nine jars is performed;
if the worship is deficient by two or three days, the bathing with twenty-five jars is performed.
Having offered the rice mixed with jaggery as before, one should worship the Auspicious One;
specifically, one should perform worship and offer a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra.
On the fourth day, the fifth day, and the day endowed with offerings,
there shall be a ritual ablution with fifty jars in due order.
Having performed sixty-four [breaths] from six days up to ten days, one should perform eighty-one *kumbhakas*;
however, if one performs from eleven up to five [days], a loss of worship will occur.
Having established the Śiva-fire there and performed the ablution with one hundred and eight [offerings], one should perform the worship as before; the food offering (naivedya) should be twofold.

Having performed sixty-four breath-retentions (kumbhaka) beginning with six days and ending with ten days, there may occur a loss of worship if one performs from eleven up to five [breath-retentions]. || 7 ||
Having established the Śiva-fire there and performed the ablution with one hundred and eight [vessels], one should perform the worship as before; the food offering (naivedya) should be twofold.

Having offered the śikhā-mantra one hundred times, one should present milk-rice (pāyasa). However, in the event of a deficiency in worship, for the duration of a month, three hundred water-pots (kalaśas) must be provided.
Having offered the heart-mantra one hundred times, [one should perform the rite];
however, when there is a deficiency in the bali offering at twilight, one should perform it twice elsewhere.
When there is a deficiency in the bali offering at both twilights, one should perform it twice for the other twilight as well.
(From PDF 140, p.
792) If the offering of oblations (*bali*) is omitted at the three junctions of the day, one should perform a ritual bathing (*snāpana*) there.
If the interruption of the oblations occurs for two days and continues until the end of the month, [one must perform the rite].
Having prepared the Śiva-fire as before, the preceptor should perform the ablution one hundred and eight times and offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the Śiva-mantra.
One should perform the ritual ablution with exactly one hundred and eight water-pots;
two *bhāras* of food offerings should be presented, and the festival should be celebrated for a single day.
Even upon contact with women or *śūdras*, or even upon contact with a *caṇḍāla*, [the rite must be performed].
The ablution (snapana) is performed with the twenty-five [syllables], while the Śiva-mantra is recited one hundred times. || 15 ||
But at the time of the circumambulation of the offering, [one should worship] either the image or the linga itself. || 16 ||
If [the image] should become cracked, moved, split, destroyed, or severed,
one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) right there, or else in the middle of the temple.
Having performed the bali offering and the circumambulation there as before,
or else, having performed it as before, one should offer oblations a hundred times with the Śiva-mantra.
Afterwards, [one should perform] one hundred and eight [offerings];
there, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and offer one hundred oblations with the root mantra alone.
Afterwards, the Guru should mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times. (20)
At that time, if there is no lamp, remain there and then offer the bali;
having taken up the lamp once more, perform the remaining circumambulation. || 21 ||
If the food offering (*naivedya*) is omitted, [the penance] is double. (pdf 141, p.
793) But if the daily fire-ritual (*nityāgnikārya*) is omitted, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*).
But listen now specifically to the rule for atonement regarding festivals. || 23 ||
If the bull-sacrifice is omitted, the hoisting of the banner is omitted;
if the banner-pole is omitted, the staff and the altar are omitted.
But if it is devoid of its banner and bell, fallen, or lacking its limbs, and likewise devoid of the garland of *darbha* grass... || 25 ||
But if the offering of the sprouts is omitted, and the sacrifice with the weapon-mantra is likewise neglected; || 26 ||

If it is devoid of mantras, devoid of ritual actions, lacking the darbha-grass enclosures, lacking the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), lacking the ritual jar (kumbha), or devoid of water; || 27 ||

But [the rite] is rendered defective if it lacks jewels and gold, or if it lacks the sacrificial grass-bundle (kūrca) and the thread; likewise if it lacks the seat (viṣṭara), the enclosing sticks (paridhi), or the cloth.
[Regarding] the offering of food and so forth:
if there is a mixture of substances used for worship that have become stale between the linga and the image,
or if the image falls during the time of the ritual, it becomes deficient in its constituent parts.
During a festival in that village, or when a death occurs during the Manyaka rite,
the night of the full moon is terrifying, as is the night when one is consumed by fire.

When there is an absence of the protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*), when there is a confusion of mantras, and when the teacher’s fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is deficient— when such things arise, they cause harm to the villages and other settlements. (33)
(From PDF 142, p.
794) But when the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣayāga*) is omitted, the cows will perish without a doubt.
Having performed the ceremonial bathing of the bull, one should adorn it with scents and flowers. (34)
One should offer mung beans... [and so forth]. Then, having performed the propitiatory fire-sacrifice (*śāntihoma*) according to the rule, the wise one should install [the image].
However, if it is devoid of the banner and the altar, it brings fear to the practitioners of mantra. (36)
Then, having performed a pacifying oblation (śāntihoma), one should perform the re-consecration in the event that the cord is lost, the banner is broken, or it is destroyed or fallen. || 37 ||

[Having performed the ritual for] the flagstaff... [and having performed] the pacifying fire-oblation (*śāntihoma*), one should then worship the devotees. However, if it falls while lacking a bell, there will be the destruction of children. (39)
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should mutter the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) one hundred times;
having sprinkled [the bell] with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should then rejoin it.
O Śambhu, one should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed and also strike the drum (bherī).
But during the time of the heat, when the drum is broken, or when it falls, or even upon the bursting of its leather, one should predict the destruction of the crops. || 42 ||
Having recollected the mantra of the colors and offered the oblation, one should mutter that [mantra] a hundred times;
afterwards, having taken hold of another according to the ritual rule, one should strike him.
If [the village] is possessed of these unfavorable characteristics, the destruction of that village will occur. || 44 ||
(From PDF 143, p.
795) He who should perform what is devoid of valid authority or introduce what lacks valid authority must first perform a *śānti*-oblation and then carry out the respective ritual action. (45)
If the sacrificial altar on the vedi is deficient, there will undoubtedly be the destruction of the crops;
therefore, having purified it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
But if the jars placed in the middle of the sacrificial hall [are damaged], || 47 ||
The king shall obtain invincibility against fear from enemy armies within his kingdom;
as before, this is achieved through the ritual jars within the sacrificial hall according to the prescribed rules.
Starting from that very day, one should perform the festival again;
and if [the image] is burnt by fire through negligence, one should arrange [the rites] in sequence as before.
When the *sṛksṛva* is lost, people are afflicted by fever and death. || 50 ||
A great disease constantly afflicts the inhabitants of the village;
one should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the Triyambaka mantra.
If the darbha-garland is missing and a drought ensues,
one should recite the root mantra a hundred times and then re-attach the darbha-garland.

And when the materials for the fire-oblation (*homa*) are lacking, there will be drought and [other calamities]. The wise one should perform the oblation with those very materials according to the previously mentioned procedure.
However, if the weapons are destroyed by a thief, it brings about a terrifying danger.
One should perform a fire oblation (homa) one hundred times with the three-syllabled mantra;
having done so, one should sprinkle [the object] with auspicious water (śivāmbhas) that possesses the proper characteristics.
(From PDF 144, p.
796) But when it is devoid of the eight auspicious signs, there is the destruction of the people;
O Lord... [text fragment]. || 56 ||
If the rite of planting the sprouts is omitted and the seed-vessels and other implements are lacking, there will undoubtedly arise a great disease and the destruction of the crops. (57)
Having offered oblations with the thousand-root mantra, one should worship the devotees;
thereafter, one should perform the rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) using vessels such as *pālikās* that possess the proper characteristics.
And when the ritual of the weapons (astra-yāga) is omitted, a great plague breaks out;
therefore, one should perform the oblation to the forms (mūrti-homa). || 59 ||
And if the placement of the water-pot is omitted, famine will certainly arise. || 60 ||
Then, having performed the *mūrtihoma*, one should offer oblations one hundred times with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*),
especially in cases of negligence or when the sacrificial lamp has gone out.
The destruction of crops and even madness will certainly arise;
having offered a hundred oblations with the terrible mantra, [the result follows]. (62)
Famine arises when there is an interruption of the fire in the sacrificial pit.
Having placed ashes, charcoal, and fire before him as before,
he should offer fuel-sticks, sacrificial porridge, and parched grain with the root mantra.
Having offered a hundred oblations for each [deity], one should offer the *vyāhṛti* at the end of the substances;
especially so when the sacrifice lacks a lamp or in the event of negligence.
There will certainly be the destruction of crops and madness will arise;
having offered a hundred oblations with the terrible mantra, one should then light a lamp.
Having again fashioned the trident-weapon, one should install it according to the prescribed rite;
and in the case of a fracture in any other limb, one should perform the rejoining once more. (78)

The ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) and the breaking [of the vessel] at the time of consecration (pratiṣṭhā) must be performed even when there is the destruction, splitting, or falling of the ritual weapons (āyudha). || 79 ||
If [the vessel] is lost or broken, it must be replaced with one possessing the previously mentioned characteristics;
for if the vessel for the bali offering is missing, wealth and grain will perish. || 81 ||
Having offered a hundred oblations with the *ghora-mantra*, one should accept a new vessel;
however, if it is devoid of the *bali* and *tāla* rites, it will become entirely unpleasant.
One should recite the Mūrti-mantra and the Mūla-mantra [one hundred times each]; likewise, one should recite each of the five Brahmans and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) one hundred times.
Having lit the lamp twice as many times, one should perform the remaining rites of the bali offering.

When the transgression of time has occurred, or when the offering of the *bali* or the vehicle [is neglected], the destruction of that village is declared; one should offer a hundred oblations with the mantra of the [respective] caste. (85)
During a festival, if the vehicle is lacking, the king shall meet his death. || 86 ||
Having offered a hundred oblations with the *varṇa-mantra*, one should perform the auspicious bathing of the *kautuka*;
furthermore, upon departing, one should not perform a circumambulation of the village.
If at that time there is quarreling or fear from thieves, one should offer a hundred oblations of root-seeds (*mūlabīja*)... [and so forth].
(From PDF 146, p.
799) One should worship the *liṅga* with materials that have been left over from previous offerings and are thus mixed. || 89 ||
Fear from enemy armies and disease shall prevail among kings;
by offering one hundred oblations with the Aghora-weapon mantra and performing the lustration rite twenty-five times, [these evils are averted].
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should mutter [the mantra]...;
the destruction of the presiding deities of the site (*vāstu-rāja-adhideva*) may occur in an instant.
One should perform a ritual bathing (*snapana*) there, and then cause the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited.
Then, having performed a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should perform the re-consecration;
however, one should abandon a [liṅga] that is broken at the head, arms, or feet, or one that has been fixed in place. || 93 ||
For one who cuts the nails, the fingers, or the ornaments;

likewise for a Śūdra within the period of initiation (dīkṣā); and for one who transgresses the word of the Guru—there will undoubtedly be the displacement from their station for all those residing in that village. || 95 ||
Having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
one should then have the image bathed and offer a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra.
During the festival,
one should offer oblations a hundred times each for the Varṇa-mantra, the [principal] mantra, and the Astra-mantra;
at that time, one should assign the protection of the world to Īśāna.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra, one should recite the Vyomavyāpin mantra a hundred times;
however, if the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) is omitted, there will be danger from fire.
(From PDF 147, p.
800) But when the seed of the primal nature [is affected] by a hundred...
(?), and when the palace is consumed by fire, there shall be fear of hunger for the village dwellers.
If one offers a hundred oblations without mantras, one should then bathe the auspicious seed-syllable.
If the commencement of war is omitted, there will undoubtedly be a destruction of crops;
therefore, having offered a hundred oblations with the upward-facing wheel, one should proceed with the start of the war.
And for all women who are devoid of the protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*), there is destruction;
[the rest of the verse is illegible].
Thereafter, one should cause the ceremonial bath (snapana) to be performed and then carry out the consecration (abhiṣecana).
If the flagpole is devoid of its descent-rite, that results in great sin;
having offered a hundred oblations with the Praṇava, one should thereafter raise the flag.
For one who is devoid of the ritual of pure bathing, there will undoubtedly be a drought;
[this applies even if] a hundred men [are present]. || 106 ||
Having offered a hundred oblations with the Varṇa-mantra, one should then perform the ceremonial bathing.
And on the very next day, one should perform the ritual at the eastern bathing place (pūrvatīrtha);
otherwise, there will be deficiency in the kingdom and the destruction of the villages. || 108 ||
Then, having performed the oblation to the quarters (diśāhoma), one should cause the pacificatory oblation (śāntihoma) to be performed;
[the rest] is as previously stated.
Having offered oblations while worshipping with the root mantra, one should thereafter perform the ritual dismissal (udvāsana).
(From PDF 148, p.
801) If the Caṇḍayāga is omitted, there will be fear from the armies of enemy kings;
one should therefore perform the ceremonial bathing of Śambhu and carry out the Caṇḍayāga. || 111 ||
Due to the fault of confusion regarding the tantras, death, disease, and other calamities arise;
[the rest of the verse is missing]. || 112 ||
And one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara, who brings about all peace.
But regarding the practice concerning what is not the truth, listen to the rule for atonement:
having touched one who has not been initiated into one's own caste, one should perform a bath with ashes. 114.
In the intermediate births, one should perform the two-fold ritual bath;
[regarding] the Caṇḍālas... [text fragment]. || 115 ||
Thus, two types of bathing have been declared; one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
If a foul odor should come with the wind, one should turn away from the tip of the nose;
likewise, having touched cow dung, one should quickly recite the five-syllabled mantra.
Having performed [the rite] for those initiated by his own caste according to his desire, the wise one [attains] even in the sky... || 118 ||
A wise man should feed the food of a king and recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred times;
having eaten the food of a Vaiśya, he should likewise recite it one thousand times in due order.
Having eaten the food of a Śūdra out of desire, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
if one eats it continuously for a month, that [penance] is prescribed for a Śūdra.
If he is joined with a Śūdra woman, he should always behave like a Śūdra;
for sexual union with a Śūdra woman, he should offer a hundred oblations into the fire.
(From PDF 149, p.
802) If one touches a woman during her menses, having offered oblations and bathed, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times;
having recited the Varṇa-mantra one hundred times, one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara. 122.
At the time of eating without a lamp, one should recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times;
but having eaten, at the time of the [deity's] vision, one should utter the heart-mantra according to one's ability.
One should remember the Lord of the gods; by bathing with ashes, one will become purified.
One should avoid garlic, fish, meat, and the remnants of others' food.
But having consumed [forbidden food] through negligence, one should recite the mantra of the caste (varṇa) one hundred times;
furthermore, one should eat the remains of the food of the senior preceptor (jyeṣṭhācārya), which bestows all accomplishments (sarvasiddhi). || 125 ||
If one recites the Heart Mantra over salt placed in the middle of water during the Vaśantaka period, every affliction is destroyed. || 126 ||
Having uttered the word "puccha" (tail) and the command "feed," while reciting the heart-mantra;
and having heard the uninitiated person's devotion, while reciting the heart-mantra.
Listen to the rules for expiation for minor sins and the great sins:
the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and likewise the theft of gold. (128)
Disregarding the Guru’s word is equivalent to the killing of a cow and constitutes one of the five great sins;
therefore, having meditated upon the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti within the abode of the Teacher, [one should perform penance].
Or one should observe a vow of silence for half a month while eating delicious food;
having drunk the water of the Supreme Lord, one should perform ritual bathing at the three junctions of the day.
Having recited the Varṇamantra one hundred times, one should perform the gift of all one's possessions;
one should constantly recite the three-syllabled mantra while standing in water reaching up to the neck.
Having meditated, one should perfume [the object] three times and worship the Guru as a deity;
constantly reciting the name-mantra, one should speak with the seal of knowledge (jñānamudrā). 132.
(From PDF 150, p.
803) One is liberated from all sins and shall attain the state of Dakṣiṇā.
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe in order the impurities resulting from birth and death. 133.
Purification for a Brahmin occurs after ten days; for a Kṣatriya, after twelve days;
for a Vaiśya, purification is after a fortnight; and for a Śūdra, purification is after a month. (134)
Established in his own duty and possessing right knowledge, he should dispel the darkness of the ignorant;
at that very moment the knower is purified, while the ignorant one suffers from grief and distress.
In the Ūrdhva-tantras, there is no impurity of birth resulting from sacraments nor the state of being a ghost;
therefore, with every effort, one should initiate [the disciple] into the Śaiva path in the Ūrdhva tradition.
For consecrated kings, there is neither birth-impurity nor death-impurity;
they are liberated from all defects and the *kṛtyā* spell by means of the seal of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*). || 137 ||
Having meditated and recited, one should always perform worship and recite the name-mantra;
by always reciting the name-mantra, one shall destroy all defects. || 138 ||
I shall describe the expiation for defects arising from faults and so forth in the *liṅga*; listen to them in due order.
When the *liṅga* is cracked, cut, broken, or likewise split; (139)
Whether the staff has fallen, or been swept away by the current of a river, or even raised up by an elephant, or stolen by thieves or madmen; 140.
Having installed that auspicious liṅga there, one should worship it as before;
then, having set up a thousand-pitcher (sahasrakalaśa), one should perform the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
One should join the stream of the river that has severed the womb with four staffs;
one should worship the invisible root-linga as the ninefold linga.
One should quickly establish that auspicious object, which brings about all prosperity, in its proper place;
having recited the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra) one hundred times, one should perform a sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
But when the retinue is destroyed, one should protect it as before; if the *liṅga* has moved due to negligence, one should re-establish it auspiciously as before. (151, p. 804) [Verse 144]
Having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred times, he should offer milk-rice (pāyasa).
The linga previously fashioned for him is the "enclosure-linga" (prākāra-liṅgaka).
The signless state (aliṅga) is to be known as the increase of the invincible king;
it is called Khaṇḍatuṇḍa, and there is no fault in its extraction.
One who has performed the rites as before should place [the vessel] on the side within the great boundary;
having offered a hundred oblations with the Varṇa-mantra, one should recite the Śikhā-mantra a hundred times.
If a *liṅga* is installed in an improper location, the king shall incur invincibility; therefore, with every effort, one must not place a *liṅga* that has another [object] at its side. 148.
Furthermore, a linga situated in the middle of a rampart that was installed by an enemy brings fear to the king and the kingdom, as well as suffering, yet it causes the king himself to prosper. (149)
However, one who stands by its side, acting according to the donor's wish, should not move the Śivaliṅga, whether it be poorly situated or well-situated. (150)

Whatever statement there may be regarding the primary *liṅga*, and whatever [statement] there may be for another, the movement of that other *liṅga* brings about the prosperity of the king and the kingdom. (151)
At that time, O Maheśvara, one should install the liṅga as previously described;
one should cause garments and other articles to be given to the devotees and their attendants.
Now, I shall describe the pacification rite known as the "Miraculous" (adbhuta) for the removal of defects, when the linga becomes discolored or when the image weeps. (153)
The twenty-fifth [rite] is the ceremonial bath (snapana); one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the western direction.
With fuel-sticks of Apāmārga, one should recite the Varṇa-mantra one hundred times.
One should perform a festival for three days, and the defect of color is destroyed. In the event of the weeping of an image, one should likewise perform a fire sacrifice (homa) prior to that. (155)
One should offer three thousand oblations with fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood using the mantra "śaṃ ca me"; thus one should perform a single-day festival.
One should perform a bath with a thousand jars and offer double the quantity of oblation when the temple has fallen, been broken, or when the sacred tree has been turned into firewood. (157)
If a deer helplessly enters the palace while a garland of lamps is burning, and such an omen as this occurs, there will be danger to the kingdom for the king. (158)
And for the purpose of pacifying those defects, one should perform a fire offering (homa) in the northeast;
one should offer a hundred oblations of *aśvattha* wood with the mantra of one's own caste (*varṇa*). || 159 ||
One should hold a festival for three days and perform the worship of devotees during an earthquake,
when the quarters of the sky appear ablaze, or upon the appearance of a second sun.
If a comet appears during the day when the stars have arisen, or at night when the bow of Indra [the rainbow] is present,
there will be the destruction of people upon the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism and the fish.
For the purpose of pacifying those defects, the preceptor should perform ten thousand fire-oblations (homa) in a pavilion constructed in the southeast,
using the Tryambaka mantra.

The materials for the oblation are as previously stated; with fuel-sticks made from the Plakṣa tree, one should perform the rite of pacification in due order for a full month to bring about the cessation of defects.

If an anthill is seen at the beginning of the temple hall and other such structures, when the temple has been built according to the rules for jewels and is supported by honey-colored [materials], [it portends misfortune]. 164.
When the two Piṅgalī tubes have been inserted inside the temple,
one should lead them out from that location and fill [the area] with pure soil.
Having sprinkled [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the pacifying fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma).
One should construct an auspicious pavilion (maṇṭapa) in front of the deity, in the northeast. (166)
There, with this path of fuel-sticks, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) three times a day for seven days or three days, offering a thousand sticks every day. || 167 ||
Uttering the mantra for the sacrificial fee, "namo namo yad asya," one should offer a hundred oblations with the auspicious mantra that pacifies all defects.
Having doubled [the merit] with oblations, one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara;
and according to the prescribed rite, one should cause a jar of cool water to be placed upon the crown of the head.
One should perform the consecration with ghee and milk according to one's capacity, especially so;
and one should also perform the consecration with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the method previously described.
Having recited the Īśa-mantra one hundred times, one should then recite the root-mantra one hundred times.
[This applies even if] the mirror has moved, become worn out, or indeed fallen.
If it is broken or devoid of luster, one should cast it into water or upon the ground;
then, taking a new mirror, one should establish it with the Varṇa-mantra.
One should worship Śambhu as before for the prosperity of the king and the kingdom;
he is attended by the four Vedas in the four directions, beginning with the east. (173)
One should perform the ceremonial bath according to the extent of one's means,
using the accomplished five products of the cow as well as the five nectars.
One should consecrate the pure food with the water of coconuts, as well as with fruits such as jackfruit, and with turmeric, emblic myrobalan, and other such items.
After purifying it with ashes, one should then worship Dakṣiṇeśvara with pure offerings;
at the conclusion of that, it is prescribed that twice as much sacrificial oblation (havis) should be given.

807) Thus has been declared this rite for pacifying [misfortune], which destroys all calamities;
wherever this pacification is performed, there wealth and grain increase. (177)
For the sake of increasing longevity, health, good fortune, victory, and prosperity, and for the purpose of the advancement of the king and the kingdom, this expiation has been declared by me. (178)
The expiation has been declared; now hear the rule for the fruit-sacrifice.
Thus ends the chapter on expiation.
Having seen Rudra and honored him with a prostration as one who is like unto himself,
one is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Śiva. (1)
One who has traveled from afar, exhausted by the journey, circumambulates a temple of Śiva; though that fatigue leads to the fulfillment of one's purpose, it brings about the supreme goal. || 2 ||

Just as one offers salutation according to the respective deity, so too should one who performs circumambulation during festivals or at the time of making offerings become worthy of honor in the worlds. (3)
At every step, one attains the fruit of the horse sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
He who offers flowers and water for the feet rejoices among the flowers of the land and the flowers of the water.
That man who desires to establish a grove dedicated to the deity becomes wealthy, glorious, and highly honored in this world. (5)
One who possesses yoga should give ten thousand [cows] to a learned Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires;
by bathing in the water from my feet, one obtains that same fruit.
One should bathe the Lord of the Gods with the five products of a tawny cow (pañcagavya) mixed with water infused with kuśa grass; the merit shall be equal to that of giving ten million cows.
One should dwell for three nights in the region of one's guru or in the presence of that deity;
endowed with various enjoyments, one is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 8 ||
Whoever should give a bell for incense, his fame shall spread throughout the earth;
and whoever should especially give garments, ornaments, and so forth— || 9 ||
Endowed with various garments and diverse ornaments,
he who worships here in these worlds shall attain the state of Śiva.
He who gives land even the size of a cow’s ear, dedicated to Jyeṣṭhadevatā, becomes a sovereign ruler over the earth,
extending to the very ends of the villages.
(From PDF 156, p.
809) He who gives these [offerings] once at the proper time in the house of the teacher becomes divine like a lamp in this world and attains the state of having the same form [as the deity]. || 12 ||
One who undertakes this, as well as one who performs worship dedicated to Śiva, always obtains the fruit of all gifts, asceticism, and sacrifice; of this there is no doubt. (13)
Then, one should have a temple constructed with bricks and metals;
by means of that golden celestial chariot (*vimāna*), one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
When the site of the preceptor has been properly prepared according to the rules and the path of ritual injunctions, [one should proceed].
He attains the world of Śiva, being constantly honored by the asuras. || 15 ||
One who stays near a temple of the gods attains the same form as Śiva;
thereafter, one should know that one reaches the world of Śiva and attains the state of proximity [to him]. || 16 ||
Having fully worshipped Dakṣiṇeśvara, the Lord of Gods as prescribed in the Āgamas, he became endowed with beauty and youth, and possessed of all enjoyments. || 17 ||
Having enjoyed pleasures in the city of Śiva, he shall become a sole sovereign on earth;
this applies to one who gives even a mere māṣa of gold or silver.
Having uplifted twenty-one generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
likewise, one who serves and is devoted to his guru, and to the preceptor who dwells elsewhere. || 19 ||
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures endowed with all objects of desire,
they return here upon the exhaustion of their merit and become a sole sovereign on earth.
One should offer a single coin and attain the southern path;
for by reciting the mantra with speech and constantly remembering Sadāśiva, one attains that goal.
Having enjoyed pleasures in the city of Śiva, he became the sole sovereign of a portion of the earth;
having constructed flower-garlanded pavilions, halls, cow-pens, and temples.
(Supplemented from PDF 157, p.
810) Surrounded by many sons, he enjoys pleasures according to his desires, having meditated upon the true nature of the seat and the sitter as the Lord Dakṣiṇa. (23)
One should worship for the sake of all accomplishments and shall always dwell in my world;
he who would even give up his life for the sake of Śiva [attains this]. (24)
Sālokya, sāmīpya, and sārūpya are indeed accomplished there, on the southern side near the sacred field of Śiva. || 25 ||
A mortal who dies right there goes to the world of Śiva;
having performed worship with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he attains the supreme goal. || 26 ||
Therefore, one should always worship Śiva with every effort.
The procedure for the ripening of the fruit has been declared; now hear about the Kṛttikā-lamp rite.
Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the ripening of the fruit in the great tantra called the Makuta.

On the eighth, the fifteenth, and the fourteenth days, as well as on the lunar nodes (parvan), at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṅkrānti), at the equinoxes (viṣuva), during eclipses, and likewise at the solstices (ayana). || 1 ||

During initiation and the rites up to the installation, as well as during sprinkling, festivals, at the conclusion of a sacrifice, under auspicious constellations, and when performing auspicious mantra-siddhi; || 2 ||

one should lay down the central [thread] measuring twenty-five [units], with two feet on each side of the *mātṛ*.

Milk, curd, and ghee, as well as fruit—specifically plantain, coconut, mustard, and sesame. || 18 ||

provided with a *kūrca* and a mechanical support (*yantra*), and joined with gold.
Having established the seal of peace (śāntamudrā) and joined the seal of knowledge (jñānamudrā),

Having established the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the other offerings up to the eight Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*),

The worship performed that many times is known as "attaining the sacred ford" (āptatīrtha);
this should be recited with mantras by one who desires success. || 37 ||
That which was to be said has been said together; indeed, it was spoken along with what was previously mentioned.

the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are auspicious in three hundred and eight [vessels].

Likewise, the Śyāmīkara-homa, followed by the golden pitcher (svarṇakumbha),

One should install the six forms with water alone;

yellow orpiment, as well as amārja, collyrium, and realgar.
Saurāṣṭra, Siktava, and likewise Gaurīka—

having placed the letter *ga* in the center, one should place the letter *gha* in the north. || 14 ||
Having placed the letter Ṅa in the center, one should place the letter Ca in the directions;
having placed the letter Cha in the eastern direction, [one should place the others accordingly]. || 15 ||
Having placed the letter Ṭa in the center, one should place the letter Ṭha in the southwest (Nairṛta).

The three outer circles have been described; now hear the sequence for the middle circle. Having placed the letter *ḍa* in the west, one should place the letter *ḍha* in the direction of the wind (the northwest).

Having placed the letter *ṇa* in the west and the letter *ta* in the north, one should place the letter *tha* in the west and the letter *na* in the south. Having placed the letter *pa* in the south, one should assign the letter *pha* as the *śakti*. || 19 ||
One should place the letter *la* at the western corner of the hexagon;
having placed the letter *ha* in the west, one should place the letter *ma* in the center.
In the triangle with a central trident, one should place Hara, Māyā, and Jaya in the three corners.
O Giver of Boons, one should place the fiery trident-enclosure, an ocean of thirty-five kalās,
as the outermost layer, containing the excellent seed-syllable of the trident.
(From PDF 204, p.
859) In the northeast, from the interior and so forth, [one should face] one's own [direction]...

One should place the Vaiśya facing north and the Śūdra facing west;
as for those of other castes, one should place them in the intermediate corners.
O Maheśvara, I shall describe the locations and the forms of those respective seats:

Four-armed and three-eyed, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
